I trust I can rely on your vote

paras.t: I've been down this path before. Amy and I packed the garage with dried pasta, tinned tomatoes, cannellini beans and bottled water during Convid. Withdrew a couple of grand in cash from the bank. Bought some physical gold and silver coins. We were told The Great Reset was coming. The New World Order. They were going to pull the plug. A false flag, a psyop. A global war, perhaps a cyber attack, another mutation that 'targeted the vaccinated’ or another novel virus — The Big One this time — something that, to paraphrase Bill Gates, will really get our attention.

We ended up taking half of the emergency food to the local tip as it had ‘expired’. Amy gets a bit squeamish about ‘best before’ dates. We’d gone from conversations about whether we would have to eat our dogs (I would, if it was a matter of life and death, Amy couldn’t and wouldn’t) if the global food chain collapsed, to dumping perfectly good food in landfill in the space of three years.

I’d researched what would really be needed if the lights went out and it was more than a few weeks' worth of ragu bolognese, linguine and bottled water. The Prepper guides 'essentials' lists would keep Rambo going for years. Weaponry, first aid, water purification systems. The works.

I know Dev says not to worry about stocking up. But he's not right about everything. A few extra supplies can't hurt. Just in case. People I knew and trusted were recommending stocking up. Others were going further than just a recommendation, they were insistent that we all needed Armageddon supplies. I noted that many of the extreme alarmists had curated links to survival supplies websites (paid per click-through no doubt) and ‘A word from our sponsor’ (my favourite was the wonderfully-named ‘Sgt Prepper Shop’ interludes during their video posts). It was open season for shills.
So a few cases of tinned food. Some Evian. Those 5 litre tins of Cretan extra virgin olive oil on Amazon too. Great value. Packed full of polyphenols.

We’ve got some cash too. We were going to do this anyway so win/win. They seem to have been intentionally making it harder to get hold of cash in recent weeks — banks have reduced the withdrawal limit at cashpoints in lockstep and there’s a requirement to pre-book appointments for larger withdrawals. Appointments that never seem to be available. I haven’t seen a queue at a cashpoint for years. Not that there are many left. It’s all rather odd.
I wouldn't say there was a run on the banks, but people have been visibly taking out more cash. Even the normies. But there again they’d panic bought toilet roll and Marmite.

They don’t want us stocking up on cash. Why? Is this a reason to stock up? Or a distraction? If they really didn't want people withdrawing cash, cash simply wouldn't be in the news cycle. They've been slowly getting rid of cash for years. Why the focus now? Fuck knows what’s going on. Fuck knows what’s ever going on.

That last bundle I withdrew in 2020 was long gone. A pint here, a plumber's bill there. Most of it was paid back into the bank and used to fund some crypto 'investments'. XRP skyrocketed. Then plummeted. The meme coins were a mug's game. I found that out the hard way. In those instances, what went up did come down. With a sickening thump.
Still, the gold coins safely hidden in the sock drawer are worth their weight in, well, gold. The value of which has increased steadily. That was a smart move. Very savvy.

None of what I’ve done is what Dev recommended. He messaged me early this morning. Crack of dawn. He has intel that ‘it’ may be imminent. Days, not weeks. The Valentine’s Day gematria predictions may not be far off. I sent him a link to a prepper site. Project Nomad. He treated it with the derision I expected. Anyway, I have a ten-point action list, of which I’ve ticked-off precisely zero. This is my job for this afternoon. Starting with the local AI downloads he recommends. Claude doesn’t have a local option. I’m sure he’ll understand if I’m forced to play the field.

choices.label: You have been warned
opts: Prepper list. Build a bunker. Ammo.
A bit of extra cash, some tins. Don’t go overboard.
Leave it. You’ve seen it all before. Well, maybe some bog roll.

paras.t: There was a meme doing the rounds a year or so ago. A video of this chap. I have no idea who he was. Rugged. Careworn. Probably late thirties. English James Dean vibes. Smoking a cigarette. Articulating the curse of awareness. All Nietzsche and objective ego. An appeal to others as intelligent as him. Who suffer like him. Those as edgy and paranoid as him. Not the others, not the fools.
It was so on the money. Too on the money. Contrived. Look how haggard knowing makes you. How unhappy it makes you. How alienated. How pointless knowing is.
Why has this come to mind again now?
It’s so achingly cool and perfectly sums up the plight of those who ‘have it all sussed out’.

But it’s not so cool when the mainstream catches up. When the fools finally awaken. Perhaps being two steps ahead is the point of the awareness? The ego is lured by its desire for a sense of superiority. Once a cause has been taken up by the conformists, you’re no longer a rebel. You’ve lost your cool.
But you got what you wanted, didn’t you? You were proven right. The endless research vindicated. The conspiracy theorist slurs dismissed.
So why aren’t you happy? Was being the outsider actually what it was all about?
admit it, you loved the conspiracy slurs, you lived for them.
And here I am. Half-heartedly prepping for Armageddon we warned about, whilst the skilled TV watchers who spent years refusing to listen, run around in a state of panic.

Everyone’s feed has been showing them the shortages, the queues, the fear. Mainstream, and all the flavours of alt-media in alignment. BBC showing queues at petrol stations going round the block. Sky interviewing shoppers incandescent with rage that Lidl had run out of bottled water. Grifters grifting. Barely a sheet of paper between laughable conspiracy theories and plausible analysis. Jenny Wilson on twitter thinks the conspiracy theorists should take a day off. But look through her feed (if indeed she exists as a human) she also thought the unvaccinated should have been imprisoned and we came out of lockdown too soon.

The harsh truth is that I have no idea what’s going to come to pass over the coming days, weeks, months. Just look at the news cycle. Fear with a side order of placation and reassurance. Chaos, half-truths, conflicting reports. Stay calm, it’s under control, take sensible precautions, heightened threat levels, queues for petrol, reduced cash withdrawal limits, robust and resilient defence levels, markets crashing, markets stable. And the fact is, this sense of not knowing which way is up isn’t so different from the status quo. In fact it’s no different. We’ve been conditioned to accept chaos as the norm. Desensitised. Rabbits in the headlights.

My gut instinct is that the chances of this event being anything other than next week’s chip paper are slim. But whatever the extent of the problem, the solutions are baked in. Cyber attack. No cyber attack. Another lab leak. What difference?
The ludicrous thing is, part of me just thinks ‘bring it on’ — roll out v2 of the pandemic playbook. Give us another lockdown. Do something. You know the meme. Do something.

Flood it again. You know that meme too no doubt? The Chinese water torture is driving me crazy. I want them to overreach. Show their hand. Bring forth rebellion and non-compliance. But they’ll have a solution for that too. Checkmate all the way up.
Knowing — small tick.
Doing — even smaller tick.
Mattering — big red cross.

Anyway, the larder is stocked, the freezer full to capacity. I got a couple of bottles of Sipsmith gin whilst I was at it. A tenner off with Clubcard. Amy managed to get a couple of jerry cans of petrol and a hundred litres of heating oil. The wind-up torch has been dug out of the shed.
The most token of token efforts.
Sgt Prepper would be rolling on the floor with laughter.

And then, as if by magic. Just before Valentine’s Day, they pull a different sort of massacre out of the playbook. Sorry to sound like that guy, but really? Two dead. Allegedly. Birmingham. Outside a primary school. Two young kids. Machete attack.

Guess what everyone is suddenly talking about? The cyber story hasn’t been debunked — it’s being buried under something the algorithm is hardwired to amplify. Grief, outrage, counter-outrage, the moderation debate, the vigil, the political statements.
The manipulation on all sides is painful to watch — the rage served to both camps, the bodies still warm and the engagement metrics already climbing.
The familiar disgust-exhaustion cycle. It’s painfully easy to see through and yet you can’t help but be drawn in, to feel the emotions. Despite yourself. Just as intended.
And the biggest horror? There’s nothing we can do about any of it.
Amy will be dismayed, disgusted, in floods of tears. Dev will ignore the noise and look for the signal. I suspect Rupert will assume it’s staged.
I wonder what @jennywilson89 will make of it?

choices.label: You have been wronged
opts: Cry
Get Mad
Get Even

paras.t: Bloody February. Perpetual rain. White skies every day. Not cloudy. White. Not freezing, but certainly big coat weather. Too hot in the woolly hat. Too cold without it. The dogs don’t care. The muddier the better. Olive is obsessed with sticks at the moment. She’s a funny thing. Wilf thinks she’s weird. He’s old and wise. Sticks are for babies. Sniffing is where it’s at.
We’ve had log fires every night. Stews. Winter fuel. Red wine, but we’ve been trying to share a bottle rather than one each.

This evening we’ve got more of the same. A Friday that feels like a Wednesday. Just the two of us tonight, the children either at parties (Sam, George and Chloe) or with their boyfriend (Emilia). It’s only five o’clock but it feels much later. The dogs have been walked, the mud cleaned off them, dried off, and are enjoying their pre-dinner snooze. Six o’clock is their feeding time, regular as clockwork. They’ll get up from their beds at five-to and wander round the kitchen expectantly.
We’ve had a lamb shoulder slow cooking in the oven all afternoon. Moroccan style. Red onions, red peppers, chickpeas, smoky with paprika and ras el hanout. One pot. Easy.
I scroll through the doom-feed whilst Amy goes for a soak in the bath. I put some music on Sonos. Panic seems particularly apt.
Could life ever be sane again?
I’ll wait until she’s back before opening the wine. Or shall I open the bottle and take her a glass for the bath? No. I’ll wait.

The level of cyber attack fear has been dialled down a notch or two. Attention has turned to the Birmingham murders. Two days since the event and still no official announcement about the suspect, other than police press conferences in which the public are asked to desist from speculation whilst enquiries are ongoing. I’m sure you can imagine the manner of delivery and intonation of Deputy Chief Constable Higgins? Obviously this request has ramped up speculation, gossip, theory and counter-theory.
There are multiple mainstream articles helping to defuse the cyber threat too. Fewer social media posts showing tins of baked beans and toilet roll in garages.
As if to prove the point, Amy comes back from her bath and tells me about her chat with her Mum. All about the murders. Asking if Amy had the latest. What can be done to stop this happening?
‘She didn’t even mention the cyber attack today. Last week it was all she talked about.’
I snigger, in what I imagine is a quite annoying manner, uncertain what to say.
‘You think the threat has gone away?’

I open a bottle of red (a German Pinot Noir) whilst considering my reply. Any annoyance my snigger caused now forgotten about as she smiles that ‘about to have my first sip of wine of the day’ smile that I know so well.

‘Who knows? I’d question whether there was ever actually an elevated threat at all. I’m not saying there wasn’t one. There’s always one. It’s just that our attention was being drawn to it. There are attacks against companies, individuals, the state every day. Hackers blackmailing, terrorists making demands, modern warfare. Asperger’s kids fucking about WarGames style on AI in their bedrooms. Some are widely reported, others aren’t. And there have been cyber security conferences and cyber resilience training exercises for years. Nothing new.’
‘So why now?’

‘The million dollar question. Three possibilities as I see it. One. A genuine threat from a state or non-state actor that intelligence has uncovered and is trying to neutralise. Even a new AI model turning on us. Who knows? The governments and media hedge their bets in reporting it - switching from ‘raised levels’ and ‘sensible degree of preparedness’ to we got this but we need more resilience to continue to maintain stability and control. Resilience meaning funds and surveillance. There’s no attack. There’s more surveillance.’
keep it short, Simon, you’re losing her…
‘Two. There’s no threat over and above the norm. Outcome the same. Essential that there’s more funding and surveillance.’
I carry on talking whilst checking on the lamb. Achingly tender. We could eat it with a spoon.

‘Three. False Flag incoming. Systems will go down. Internet. Banking. The lights go out for a bit. Think Covid fear but with no Amazon Prime deliveries and heating for a week instead of the threat of a deadly plague. Order will be restored but the ‘something must be done’ to prevent this happening again. It could be worse next time. The playbook is already written — the buzzwords - robust - contingencies - digital - quantum - public-private partnerships - global unity against enemies of democracy. You get the picture.’
‘Gun to the head, which one?’

‘Probably two. I mean this is essentially the narrative of the daily social media scroll. Scare story. Nothing happens. Next. But each story changes the mood of the nation, our view of reality. Opens or closes the Overton window a bit. Brings chaos, division, a distraction. People debate, argue, worry, demand solutions. And by fuck do they have the solution lined up and ready to roll.’
‘So why the cash and cannellini beans?’

‘Because…I don’t know. Does anyone? Hedging. You said gun to head. I went for the second option. The fact that we’ve now got the machete murders on the front pages makes me think I might be right. Who knows?’
‘What about Dev? You keep saying he thinks something will happen. The Valentine’s Day stuff.’

‘Dev knows what’s been put in place. The biometric payments. I mean it doesn’t take a genius to work out that new digital and financial systems are coming. But this is not about them coming at some unspecified point in the future. Dev thinks they go live this weekend. As he puts it — it’s not a prediction, it’s a fucking production schedule. But going live and being fully operational are two different things.’
‘So he thinks we’re going to start using fingerprints to pay for our shopping next week? That is so Dev.’

‘He thinks it’s the solution to a problem. The cyber attack equivalent of the vaccine rollout to end the pandemic. But they didn’t roll out the vaccines overnight. They made us wait. Ramped up the fear. Made people beg for their safe and effective freedom-giving juice.’
‘So we’ll be in lockdown again and the digital currency will be the thing that saves the day? Is that really going to happen?’

‘When you put it like that it sounds a bit ridiculous I guess. Who knows? I reckon it’s more likely that this just seeds the required solution in the public consciousness. Nudging us to accept it as necessary. Safe, secure, efficient, desirable. The new system is already turned on, we simply drift into it. Like landlines and mobiles. There wasn’t a grand ceremony and official Smartphone Day. It just happened. And now the thought of using a ring dial phone is ludicrous.’
‘So it’ll be fine then? I mean for this weekend. Our Valentine’s dinner.’
‘I guess. I mean, I don’t know. Probably.’
He did say stay close to home. I mean, we are anyway. So I won’t tell her. What difference will it make? It’ll only freak her out. And I want us to enjoy the Rully.

choices.label: Valentine’s Day
opts: Dinner Jazz
Barry White
The Sex Pistols

turns.title: The Last Night at the Fair

paras.t: Valentine’s Day. We’re staying in. Always have done. Two courses in the local gastropub will set us back two hundred quid — a couple of pints, a bottle of red, probably two. I won’t be able to resist the cheeseboard. Drive there, taxi back, pick the car up in the morning. Rigmarole. Money better spent elsewhere.

Anyway we’re both decent cooks and love cooking together. We’re a good team. I’m meat and sauces. She’s veg and presentation. We rarely argue. We don’t get in each other’s way. We giggle. We’re silly together. It keeps us young and vibrant.

The flat iron from our local butcher is insanely good. The depth of flavour of a ribeye with the melting tenderness of a fillet. I’ll cook it on the griddle, charred on the outside, rare in the middle. Maybe veering towards medium rare to keep my darling happy. Compromise. It’ll rest on a huge slab of oak chopping board. Adds a rugged, rustic charm as a table centrepiece. A bugger to wash up though. Tomorrow morning’s problem. Triple cooked duck fat chips. Steamed spinach. Tomatoes roasted in olive oil with copious amounts of Maldon and black pepper. Just normal peppercorns freshly ground from our tall artisan-made mill. We used to spend three times as much on Tellicherry. Couldn’t taste the difference. I’ll start making the Béarnaise too early. It will be perfect. Simmering on a low heat waiting for its chip dipping, meat slathering fate. Buttery, glossy, thick, speckled with fresh tarragon and sharp with white wine vinegar. I’ll nurse it, stirring slowly. I won’t take my eye off it. Until I do. Then it’ll split. I’ll remain calm, seething inside. Unless I’ve been on the gin. Doesn’t suit me. Whoever called it Mother’s ruin was on the money. Anyway I’ll thicken it up with another egg yolk or an ice cube. It’ll be fine.
After the meal

It all went to plan. Even the bloody Béarnaise split. I managed to salvage it. The wine was delightful. Our ‘treat’ wine. Rully Rouge Premier Cru Clos du Chapitre, Jaeger-Defaix. God it’s good. Silky, pure, plenty of berry fruit, but with some guts too. And yes, we’ve just opened the third bottle.

The Kitchen Disco is now in full swing. Started off chilled. A bit of background jazz. Flowed seamlessly into some Café del Mar. The early José Padilla stuff of course. I’d planned to get the vinyl out tonight. I’m an avid collector. Well I was. I can’t remember the last time I bought an album. I still tell everyone how digital music is inferior to the analogue sound of vinyl LPs. The artwork. A more engaging listening experience. Warm and natural. Superior dynamic range. Full-album appreciation. Stories told over multiple tracks. Tactile. Real.
I can’t remember the last time I put one on the turntable.

So here we are sitting on stools by the kitchen island. We’ve been playing ‘song tag’ — Amy chooses first, then me, then back to Amy. Spotify Premium played on Sonos Play 5. Not cutting edge, but sounds good to me. We’re now at the dancey stage of proceedings. She chose Higher States of Consciousness. I replied with Smack My Bitch Up. Love The Prodigy. A romantic choice for Valentine’s Day! We’re now listening to Insomnia.
actually I’m starting to tire, the thought of sleep is beginning to appeal
I’ve got the Age of Love lined up next. Jam and Spoon Watch Out For Stella Mix, naturally. The thought of those hypnotic, otherworldly beats at the start makes my spine tingle.
‘It’s taking its time to play, what the fuck’s happening?’ Amy demands.
Starlink has been a bit hit and miss today, but most of these songs are all saved in our Spotify Library. This ain’t our first Sonos rodeo.
‘Wheel of death on the phone. Weird. I’m sure it was in a playlist in the Library? Sod it. I’ll get it out on vinyl. It’ll sound better too.’
Bloody technology.

I rummage through the collection. I know it’s in here somewhere. I’d dumped the piles of vinyl in a random order on the shelf when we moved house three years ago (wait four, no five years ago. Where did all the time go?) and promised myself that I’d soon reorganise it into its usual orderly glory. Another entry to add to the list of things that never happened.

Found it. Eventually. I take it out of its sleeve, a million memories of top-off, wide-eyed, sweaty nights released with it. Onto the turntable it goes. The familiar plop as the spindle emerges through the hole. I hear my needle hit the groove (mental note, Stone Roses next).
Age of Love hits its angelic voices crescendo.
Remember we played together…
I’m dancing, eyes closed. My body in 2027. My mind in 1995. The dying years of The Before Times. Not that we knew it then. Tears well up in my eyes. My nostalgia spiral has started.
Time’s tide has smothered me. I can’t help but think of her.
I’m jolted back into the room as the final beats fade out. I head back to the turntable to load up the next track. It’s Amy’s turn really, but she won’t mind if I sneak on some Roses next.
As I flick through the collection, Amy leans over and shows me her phone. She’s been trying to send a WhatsApp but it won’t go through. She tries a text. Not sending either.
‘Try calling me?’ I suggest.
She clicks on Simon.
‘Nope. Nothing. Weird.’
I check my emails. Nothing received since just past nine.
‘Must be the start of the cyber attack,’ I mock, whilst loading up She Bangs The Drums, tucking the vinyl under my arm to perform air quotes around cyber attack.
We laugh. Both of us silently wondering whether this actually could be the event.
I smile at Amy. It feels like a weak smile, not the confident, reassuring one I meant it to be.
She’s my Rock. My Love. My Everything.

How could it ever come to pass
She’ll be the first, she’ll be the last
To describe the way I feel
The way I feel

choices.label: Late night
opts: Joy
Pain
Loss

paras.t:
Creaky noises make my skin creep
I need to get some sleep…
I can’t get no sleep

Where are you? In bed, check.
How do you feel? Neck’s sore. Note to self. I need new pillows. Mouth is dry.
I reach for my water. The glass is full. I take a big glug. It tickles my dry throat. I somehow manage not to spit it all out. I swallow it in stages.

What time is it? Actually what day is it? Feels early and maybe a Sunday. Reach for phone. It’s there, usual spot on the bedside table. You remembered to charge it before crashing out. First Brownie point of the day.
5.56am. Early doors.
And it’s Monday morning according to my phone, not Sunday.

I should check the girls’ location. Did they get back to Sophie’s after the party? Obviously Amy will have checked, but I should do my due diligence too. I turn to look at Amy. Deep sleep still. Away with the fairies, mumbling something about leaks. Or maybe it’s leeks? I’ll ask her when she wakes up. Doubt she’ll remember it. She’ll find it funny though. I look forward to seeing that smile.
I go to the ‘Find My’ App. Emilia — Last seen 7 hours ago. I swipe down to update. No change. Click on Chloe — same thing. 7 hours ago.
I remember the service being shit last night. Now I have three curves of full signal Wi-Fi reassurance. But Find My isn’t working.
I check to see if the internet is working. The BBC propaganda website first.
Nothing. I try something else…Crystal Palace blog…Nothing.
Fuck’s sake.
Is Starlink aligned? In fact, it’ll be easier to reboot the hub first. And I’ll put the kettle on whilst I’m at it.
Hub rebooted. Kettle on. Still no service.
X…just nothing. Insta…also nothing.
Weird.
Barclays App. ‘Closed for routine maintenance’
The Cyber Psyop, Day One.
Kettle’s boiled. Two mugs. Earl Grey and a spoon of sugar. Brown. Must be Demerara. Builders for me. I’m sweet enough already.

Back to the bedroom. The gentle clunk of mug on bedside table causes Amy to stir. Well, not gentle as such. Volume honed to perfection over the years — just loud enough to wake her with the knowledge that her tea hero has come to the rescue — not too loud as to be an annoyingly obvious ‘wake up and play’.
‘Morning’
‘Morning, darling. Cup of tea on the side for you.’
‘I know. My hero. I’ll make the difficult second cup.’
(It never gets old)
‘Bloody internet is still down’
‘Is it? Are the girls OK?’
‘Don’t know. I haven’t heard from them. Everything is down’
She jolts upright, reaching for the phone.
‘You’re right. Last seen 7 hours ago. Have you tried calling?’
I hadn’t.
‘No, I didn’t want to wake them,’ I replied, half truthfully. ‘They’ll be fine.’
‘What’s this, Simon?’
I got a Simon, something is amiss. She points at her phone. ‘100% — you’re fully charged.’
‘No, underneath that. The blue swirly logo — that app — ARC. What’s that? I don’t remember installing it.’
I look at my phone. I have the same logo, the same ARC app.
I click on it. It does nothing.
I look at Amy. She looks at me. I assume I have the same WTF look on my face that she does.
This is bizarre. I should message Dev. Wait, I can’t message Dev.

choices.label: ARC
choices.prompt: An app that installed itself and does nothing.
opts: Weird.

paras.t: Amy had left a half-drunk cup of tea on the kitchen worktop. It was highly unusual for her to begin her day without kickstarting herself with at least three cups, often accompanied by a few rounds of Marmite on toast.

She was worried about the girls. She was always worried about the girls. They’d be fine, they were at Sophie’s. We’d let them stay out on a Sunday night as they had a day off college today. A scheduled one. Not this. Whatever this is. They’re safe. The internet would be back up and running soon. It’d be much ado about nothing. As it always is. Well, almost always is. Without all the ‘cyber attack’ warnings and ‘increased threat levels’ we’d have simply thought the internet had crapped out. The difficult second and straightforward third cups of tea would’ve been made and drunk.

Whatever this was smacked of being an event, a happening, a stunt. Concocted. Implemented. Controlled. The ‘Story’ that the media would latch onto. ‘If it’s in the news it’s likely a ruse’. Stir up some panic, seed a bit of fear, ensure the algo-boosted X accounts throw in a smattering of ‘this is the big one’. BBC Verify, the arbiter of truth, setting everyone straight.
Some political bluster in the days to follow — ‘What we should do to make sure this cannot happen again?’

Answer — more robust verification processes, more control, more surveillance. Same as always. They’d definitely use the word ‘robust’, I’d stake my mortgage on it. And they’d definitely give more millions to Palantir or Oracle to guarantee this increased robustness.

Anyway, as I said, Amy didn’t finish her first cup. She’d panic-left the house within minutes of waking up, unshowered and in a tizz. ‘Love you, I’ll be back soon’ she’d bellowed from the open car window. I’d shouted after her, pointing out that they’d still be asleep. Probably for another five hours. If they’ve even gone to bed yet. Late night vodka and oranges and all-night-boy-chat if I know them.
But she had gone.
I put the kettle on to make myself a particularly challenging second cup and absentmindedly pick up my phone for the morning email/X/BBC headline check.

Nothing. Darkness. Of course. I knew there’d be nothing but somehow it still surprised me. The nimble-fingered unconscious info-sweep and instant dopamine hit is so ingrained. I used to wake up and have a spliff when I was at University. My first contact with the world at large a perusal of The Sun (I know, I was young and liked the, err, sport section) on the tube to central London.
Nowadays the psyops start before I’ve even had a piss.
6.07am. The clock is the only thing that’s working on my phone. Well, that and the torch. All the apps open but state various versions of ‘service unavailable’.

I try the Mac and the iPad too. Nothing. Reset the router a few more times. Starlink app opens OK — claims ‘Starlink is aligned’ — but also tells me it’s ‘Offline’ and the router is ‘unreachable’. Annoying. I had set aside the morning for sending out invoices to market traders, but this relied on Quickbooks Online, which was just hanging. Not even a courtesy ‘we’ll be back online soon’.

At least the power was on. Cup of tea number three and a couple of slices of toast. Real Patisserie ‘chewy brown’. Quite possibly the best loaf known to man. I butter it whilst it’s hot, the butter melting and collecting in the sourdough pools. A carby treat for my hangover.
Extra insulin needed, 12 units should do it.
Hardly scientific but an educated guess after years of carb-counting, trial and error.

Kate from next door knocks. She was supposed to be on a video call with an overseas client. Early start for her. She’s just checking if our internet was down too. I ask her in for a tea but she declines, wanting to go back next door and get the Teams call to work.

I check WhatsApp again. Lots of grey single ticks. No one was receiving my messages. I had one message from Vince. 1.01am. He’d obviously had issues too but it looks like it’s sorted in London now. Reassuring.

I sit in the beaten-up leather armchair in the hallway. Slurping, crunching, chewing. No phone. Just me, my thoughts, a view of the plants in the courtyard outside the front door. The olive tree had wintered well. The magnolia looking as if it would soon blossom into its early spring glory. The dogs settle at my feet. Peace.
I could get used to this. No phones. No constant connectivity.

Just as I’m starting to nod off I hear the sound of a key trying to fit into the front door lock. George is back. What the hell is he doing back just after six in the morning? He looks even more hungover than I feel. He’d been for a Valentine’s booze at the local with his mates and crashed on Thomas’s sofa. Couldn’t sleep, so decided to head home. Probably still over the limit. But it’s only a short drive down country lanes, I guess.

We confirm to one another that the internet is fucked. (His words. Actually mine too, come to think of it.) He’d tried to call Amy but was getting either nothing, straight-to-voicemail or endless ringing with no answer.

‘Have you tried the TV?’ he asks. I hadn’t thought of that. We turn it on. Just a black screen. Of course it is, we’d watched TV over the internet via an Amazon Fire TV Box for years. ‘Does this thing even have ‘normal’ TV?’ I ask George. He had no idea. He thought we did watch normal TV.
‘Cup of tea, Georgie?’
‘No thanks, I’m knackered. See you on the other side.’ He slinks off to his room.

choices.label: Network Status
opts: Don’t Panic

turns.title: I am the God of Hellfire

paras.t: What the hell is that? The most God-awful noise. Ear piercing. The dogs bark in unison. Wilf, hackles up, deep and manly followed by a growl. Olive, bemused look on her face, higher pitched and more incessant.
George bursts back into the hallway, the door somehow staying on its hinges.
‘What the…?’
He shows me his phone. The source of the sound identified. The klaxon I assumed was only ever for Emergency Alert tests and scaremongering.
UK GOVERNMENT EMERGENCY ALERT

I skim read it in disbelief. Major cyber incident…UK financial and digital infrastructure…Emergency services…card and electronic banking payments have been suspended…and then at the bottom… from the same people who brought you The Plandemic…
STAY HOME. STAY CALM.
This is really happening.
We stand in stunned silence. I reach out to grab my phone, thinking for a moment I’d been pranked. But there it is. The same message. Phone still vibrating. An exclamation mark in a red triangle.
I turned the alerts off before they did the tests a few years ago. And I didn’t get the ridiculous BBQ’s cause wildfires alert over the summer.
I look at George, confused. ‘I’m sure I had these turned off?’
He shrugs. ‘I’m sure they can send it out regardless?’
I smile a weak smile.
Yeah, of course. Who am I trying to kid?
I read it again. More slowly this time. It still doesn’t fully sink in. All I can think of is Klaus Schwab, in full Dr Evil mode—
The COVID-19 crisis would be seen in this respect as a small disturbance in comparison to a major cyber attack.

And the ending. Stay Home. Stay Calm. Why no third instruction this time? Where was the ‘Save Lives’ or ‘Control the Virus’? Has the Nudge Unit had a rethink? They’re leaving us hanging, waiting for the final command. Probably some new behavioural game theory that’s being tested — condition your victims into expecting a trio of instructions, then, at a moment of heightened tension, deliver only two. Leave them expectant, confused, immobilised.
I feel like I’m at a crucial stage of a ‘choose your own adventure’ book. But the ‘turn to page sixty-five’ options are purely in my head.
‘Why do we need to stay home?’ asks George.
‘Good question. Crisis management I guess. They don’t want hordes of civilians panicking on the streets.’
‘Won’t telling people to stay calm have the opposite effect?’
It seems Georgie has learnt something on the way.
‘Good point. Especially when the ‘stay calm’ request comes via an unprecedented emergency alert.’
‘So do we stay calm?’
‘What’s on the cover of The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy?’
‘Eh?’
‘Oh for fuck’s sake, George, how many times have I told you to read it? Don’t Panic. In capitals.’

choices.label: Stay Home
opts: Don’t Panic
Panic

paras.t: Banging at the door. Two teenage faces next to each other pushing their noses against the glass. It’s the girls. They’re back. Manic grins, eyes a mix of excitement and confusion.
I open the door and they pour in, unleashing a stream of Gen Z buzzwords - oh my days, what the hell?, OMG and other acronyms that I’m not down with the kids enough to understand.
‘Did you get it Dad?’ asks Emilia.
‘The alarm? Yeah.’ I’m aiming for reassuring fatherly meets effortless chill.
'Why did Mum come and get us so early? We had about two hours sleep’ Chloe asks grumpily. ‘What did she think was going to happen?’

I don’t bother to answer. It was largely rhetorical. Chloe knows full well than Amy would have been worried sick that she didn’t know they were safe. She was an obsessive ‘Find My’ track and tracer, message-me-when-you-get-homer.
‘I presume you girls have had no internet either?’
‘Not since, like midnight or something’. I decide not to call Emilia out on the ‘like’. Rarely a sentence goes by without one.

‘It’s so annoying’ Chloe shows me her phone. Instagram, SnapChat - both not updating. One of those bloody awful tongues-out, peace-fingered salutes selfies from a gaggle of scantily-clad girls at the pre-party the last Insta image and a message from Eddie on Snap, three kisses.
Eddie, eh? Who the hell is Eddie?
In comes Amy, noticeably less jittery now the girls have been rounded up. The dogs greet her like she’s been gone for months. They're loving this early morning kerfuffle.
‘Have you heard from Sam?’
‘No, not yet.’
‘Are you not worried?’
‘Well, not really, no more than normal. He’ll be fine. The internet is down, it’s not World War 3.’
‘I thought you’d be more, like, um, weird about this, Dad.’ Emilia clearly thought I’d be in a frenzy as one of my conspiracy predictions appeared to be coming true.

‘All that’s happened is the internet is down and the Government have sent an emergency bleep. Let’s not overreact, it’s probably nothing. No point jumping to conclusions or reacting with emotion. Let’s see what happens.’
‘I thought you’d have loads of theories, start talking about Hegelian dia-thingy and stuff.’
As if on cue, another ear-piercing klaxon sounds from everyone’s phone. Dogs barking, everyone reaching for their device. George is quickest on the draw.
‘Here’s another one. It’s different’

Remain calm. Remain indoors while situation is assessed. Initial reports indicate cyber attack limited to financial and digital infrastructure. Power, water, and essential services remain operational. Further guidance will follow.
‘Ten minutes later and they're doubling down on staying calm. Interesting.’ My mind is turning over nineteen to the dozen.
‘Cup of tea?’ asks Amy.
‘That’s the spirit’ I proclaim enthusiastically, with a slightly pompous patriotic fist-pump. ‘How very English. Stay Calm. Put the kettle on.’
We move to the kitchen. Kids in their usual seats at the table, Amy and I double-teaming the tea making.
‘Who wants eggy bread?’ Amy offers, pulling out her crowd pleaser. Sliced white bread, fried in eggs and butter topped with the unlikely-yet-delicious combo of marmite and Golden Syrup.
Three hungover ‘meees’ in unison. A ‘go on then’ from me. A blood sugar killer having already had early morning toast. But fuck it.
Despite the lack of internet connection, all three kids are glued to their phones, checking various apps, messaging services, email, refreshing, turning off and on.

‘This is so annoying’ Emilia grunts as she slams her phone down in anger. Moments after she does, the third klaxon of the day announces that the internet has been shut down as a precaution. We agree that an intentional switch off rather than a hack is good news. Of sorts.
‘If it hasn’t been hacked and it’s only turned off as a precaution, surely it’ll be back on soon?’ George asks optimistically. He’s undoubtedly thinking no internet, no TikTok, no income.

‘I guess so. How long can they shut the internet down for without riots? Mandatory Digital ID. No problem. Epstein child torture. Whatever. No TikTok for forty-eight hours and Gen Z will be on the streets. Apoplectic cold turkeys.’

A text message cuts me off mid rant. It’s Sam. He’s fine. He’s at Mike’s. I send him a thumbs up. Amy raises an eyebrow. She’d have written a side of A4 demanding all the details, how he was feeling, what his plans are, etc, etc. He’d rather the emoji.

Eggy bread demolished, another round of teas drunk, we sit around the table wondering what to do. We’re all holding onto our phones, occasionally absent-mindedly scrolling through apps that don’t work. I’m torn between going back to bed, returning to the leather chair with a book or taking the dogs for a walk. I suggest the latter. We could all go when it warms up a little bit.
‘But they’ve told us to stay indoors’ protests Emilia. She’s a bit of a goody-two shoes when it comes to following instructions. Unless they’re from her parents.
‘Actually they’ve said stay local and stay indoors, which is a bit of a conflict. Anyway if I want to go to the woods with the dogs, I will. Twelve o’clock? Who’s in?
Twelve it is. In the meantime we retreat to our rooms to shower, take stock and nurse the Valentine’s hangovers. The unmade bed looks tempting..maybe a little lie down before a shower…
The Afternoon

The day is passing slowly. We’d been to the woods. They were eerily quiet. It’s only a two minute drive down a country lane to get to the parking spot where we start the walk so we weren’t able to get much of a feel for how busy the roads were. Everything looked normal, sounded normal. But there was an touch of uncertainty, a frisson of electricity in the air. Hard to describe, a bit like those days between Christmas and New Year when you’ve absolutely no idea what day of the week it is, with a hint of early Covid what the hell is going on thrown in for good measure.
And no internet.
Just UK Gov emergency pings giving us situation updates. It seems ‘partner nations’ have reported similar disruption according to the update we’d received at eleven.
Eleven. On the dot. In fact, all of them. On the dot. Hardly live updates…

‘Interesting choice of words.’ I’d pointed out to Amy. ‘Partner nations - meaning that ‘non-partner nations’ weren’t reporting similar disruption? Meaning they’re going to blame the attack on on a ‘hostile state’ - yes I used the quotation fingers, sorry, I know it’s annoying.
‘Like Chyna' Amy replied, she loved saying China in the Trump Chyna-virus voice.

‘There’ll be up there in the betting, for sure. Iran, North Korea, unidentified non-state actors, a terrorist cell. AI gone rogue. Not forgetting the odds-on favourite, good old false flag. I can see the meme now - horse race with an Irish commentator - ‘and it’s AI Gone Rogue, it’s lead being eaten into by North Korea. China being pushed along and looks beaten. AI Gone Rogue is coming back to them. Unidentified Non-State Actors is staying on gamely…but here comes False Flag, going very easily indeed, jockey Elon Thiel has a double handful. False Flag hits the front and wins going away.’
‘Twat’
We laughed. I think it was my jockey impressions and over-the-top Irish accent that made her call me a twat. She loved it really.

Telephone calls and texts had been a bit of a lucky dip. I’d tried Mum a few times, but had no luck getting through to Spain. Amy had heard from her Mum and Dad. They’d be the only ones panicking about us. Other texts received were just versions of ‘you getting this?’ or ‘what the fuck?’ I’d tried calling Dev a few times. Well more than a few. Not compulsively though. His original number and the new ‘walls’ burner, both dead.

The most interesting emergency alert, well, to me anyway, was the one received at two-thirty confirming that ARC - Autonomous Resilience Cloud Emergency application - has auto-installed on everyone’s phone. ‘No action required’ it noted. And ‘no authorisation given’ I noted. I’d spent about twenty minutes trying to think of a witty ARC acronym that I could text to Dev, but couldn’t think of a good enough one. It’d come to me.

At the moment ARC was simply an un-clickable app with pretty teal and white logo. No functionality. Presumably they’d send a message on it soon? I’d tried pressing it a few times throughout the day, but nothing had happened. It had installed itself on the home screen of my phone, relegating Barclays to page two. Perhaps I wouldn't be needing that for a bit? ‘Closed for routine maintenance’ it declared.
Routine, eh?
4.48pm text received from Dev. I’ll read it to you in full.
you seeing this

Even for Dev this is curt. Perverse even. Of course I’m fucking seeing it. Or is there something specific he’s hinting at? Wants me to validate a thought rather than telling me? Or is he just getting me to think? Testing me?
My reply, one graced with both capitalisation and question marks, unlike his.
Emergency messages? On the dot?
No reply yet. In fact no idea if it’s even been received.

Let’s be honest, the latter half of the day had been all about the wait for the PM Press Conference scheduled for 6pm. Covid vibes revisited. The nation awaits. Families would be huddled round the telly, just like the good old days.
Kate is going to join us. She says she doesn't want to watch it alone. I reckon she just wants to hear my sarcastic commentary. Hopefully that ARC acronym will come to me before then.

The tension was ramped up by the first ARC Emergency Update. Received at 5pm with a resounding ding, noticeably less foreboding than the emergency klaxon, and dressed up in a verging on neon teal. Less aggressive than the emergency red. Welcome to the future  - ‘we’ve got this’ vibes. Maybe I’m overthinking it?
It’s now just after half-five we’ve gathered on the sofa. BBC is simply showing ‘The Prime Minister will address the nation at 6pm’.
‘How come the TV is working on BBC now? Nothing earlier. No other channels though.’ George asks.
I hadn’t thought of that. ‘Probably some emergency override I imagine. I’ll ask Dev.’
‘If they can get BBC to work, surely they get ITV to work? Love Island is on.’ Chloe asks.
‘Oh my God, yeah.’ Emilia realises she’ll miss out on seeing some new contestants arrive on the Island, or some such garbage.
‘Oh my God, yeah.’ George repeats in a mockingly airhead tone.
‘Shut up George’ the girls reply in unison.
Some things never change.

6pm approaches, still the same message on screen. No sign of the PM yet. Will they roll out the same lectern? Will the PM be alone or joined by some trusty sidekicks? The cyber version of Chris Whitty with some fear-porn or a financial Patrick Vallance presenting some bogus statistics?
Next slide please…

opts: This is really happening
Is this really happening?
This can’t be happening

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — PM ADDRESS — 18:00 GMT — 15 FEBRUARY 2027

paras.t: Good evening.

Yesterday, on Valentine’s Day, a little before midnight, a coordinated cyber attack struck the financial and digital infrastructure of the United Kingdom and twenty-two other nations. This has caused significant disruption to civilian systems in our nation and around the globe.

Here is what we know. I will not minimise it. The attack targeted the core transaction and record-keeping systems that underpin our banking and financial services. This in turn has impacted our public services and much of our daily communication. Our security and intelligence services, working in close coordination with international partners, are engaged in a comprehensive response. I chaired COBRA at six o’clock this morning and have been in continuous session since.

Here is what I want you to understand. The damage is being assessed. The infrastructure is damaged, not destroyed. We are working — with every resource available to us — to restore normal service. Our current assessment is that this will take days, not weeks.

Let me be clear about what is not affected. Our electricity grid is operational. Our water supply is operational. Our gas network is operational. Our hospitals have power. Our emergency services are coordinating. No lives are in danger from the attack itself.

Many of you will have spent today unable to reach members of your family — unable to send emails, unable to use messaging apps, unable to refresh social media or stream the news the way you would on any other day. I know how difficult this is. I know how isolating it feels not to be able to reach a son or a daughter, a parent, a friend abroad.

These services have been restricted as a precaution while our cloud infrastructure is verified. They have not been damaged. We cannot leave them running while we are not yet certain they are safe. We expect to begin restoring them in stages from tomorrow morning, as verification work completes. Telephone calls and text messages remain operational throughout. If you need to reach someone urgently tonight, please use those.

Currently we are unable to access our bank accounts. Shops and businesses are unable to process our card payments. For this reason, for the next 24 hours retail, businesses and offices will be closed. A detailed plan for the opening of essential retail, including supermarkets, will be issued shortly.
Your savings are safe. Your deposits are protected. Nothing has been lost — only temporarily made inaccessible.

Schools were closed today and will remain closed for the remainder of the week. Hospitals remain open for emergencies only; all routine and non-urgent care has been postponed, also for the remainder of the week. All public transport services are suspended for the same period of time.
Our emergency services are operational. Our military and police forces will be visible, on the streets, to ensure the safety of every one of us.

The emergency communications platform on your phones — many of you will have already received alerts through it — is functioning as designed. It will continue to be your most reliable source of verified information in the coming days.

Part of this emergency communication system is ARC. You may have seen the app automatically installed on your devices throughout the course of the day. The ARC app adds an even more robust communication channel between Government and citizens.

I have spoken this afternoon with my counterparts across the affected nations. We are united — not only in our response, but in our resolve. This was an attack on all of us. It will be met by all of us.
In the meantime, I ask just three things of you.

First: for the next 24 hours, stay local, stay safe. Do not drive, unless it is a matter of life or death. This is not a lockdown, but a request. Look after each other. Check on your neighbours. Share what you have.
Second: do not fear. We will restore these systems. We will provide answers. And we will ensure that every family in this country is supported through this period. This period of days, not weeks.
Third: please continue to follow the guidance issued through ARC, the emergency alert system and on all BBC television and radio channels.

I will address the nation again at nine o’clock tomorrow morning with a full operational update. There will be detailed updates from my colleagues in the Cabinet and experts from the National Cyber Security Centre during this period.
There are dark days, challenging days, ahead. We face them with our unique British spirit. We face them together.
Good night. And be well.

turns.title: PM Address · Day 1 Evening

paras.t: It was just the PM. Seated. Camera still, a close up shot. Only his head, upper body and hands visible. An attempt to convey the PM as being in the room with us, figuratively and physically. No lectern. More a friendly chat than lecture. The tone was direct and authoritative, but not cold. Lots of ‘we speak’. Us. In this together vibes.

We’d watched in almost complete silence. Transfixed. I’d resisted the urge to pipe up with snarky comments on a few occasions, but in all honesty I hadn’t found myself cringing or recoiling nearly as much as I thought I would. For whatever reason, I didn't feel it needed a running commentary, so I didn't give it one.
The address came over as reassuring. Detailed without being overly technical. Not condescending or dumbed down.

Days not weeks. Nothing to be overly concerned about. Power, water, etc unaffected. The loss of internet connection was simply due to it having been taken down as a precaution. Not hacked or corrupted. There was a plea for sensible, responsible behaviour. Stay local. This is not a lockdown. Be good citizens.

That said, the effect will surely not be dissimilar to a lockdown. I mean, where will people go? What is there to do? No school, no work, no payment systems functional. Other than cash of course. For those that have any. It’s just above freezing, far from the beach weather of Spring 2020. The lights are on and everyone’s at home. With central heating on full blast.

All told, it was a bit of an anticlimax. Everyone seemed to accept what was happening at face value and shrugged their shoulders. George, Chloe and Emilia returned to their rooms pretty much staring after the TV was turned off. God knows what they planned to do without phones to mindlessly scroll. They’d experienced daily TV briefings, social distancing, lockdowns and years of viral fear and daily death counters in their formative years. This was small fry in comparison. Nothing much to discuss, they just want the Internet back. Content that everything appears to be under control. Days not weeks. Normality back soon.

A few things did stand out though. To me anyway. I didn’t comment on them at the time. I knew Amy needed reassurance not deep analysis. To feel safety and relief rather than intellectual challenge, initially anyway. We’ll discuss it when she’s ready, and I know she’ll bring it up when the time is right for her.
Kate. Now there’s an interesting one. I’m intrigued to know what she made of it.

Tonight she’d been as quiet and restrained as I’d ever seen her. It was out of character. The character I knew anyway. At least the character she portrays. Not that I know her that well, but I saw her in a different light tonight. Her professional side coming to the fore perhaps?

Usually you know when Kate’s in the room. She’s extravagant in word, gesture and appearance. An extraordinary presence, a genuine smile and a dress sense that’s quirky, colourful and flamboyant that somehow avoids zany. Today she had worn a long flowing dress with a Sicilian lemon print, bright green leggings underneath, a white woollen cardigan, huge dangly slices of lemon earrings and a green and yellow striped turban-type affair on her head. About as un-wintery as you could get, yet it just looked right.

As soon as the PM started talking she became a study of concentration and contemplation. Peering into the screen. Analysing every word of the speech. Scrutinising its structure. Assessing our reaction to it.
As it ended she flipped straight back into jovial Kate mode, quick fire streams of sentences, not letting anyone get a word in edgeways. But almost no mention of the speech at all.

‘Well that’s a relief. Much ado about nothing it seems. You guys are so lovely, thanks for having me over. I’m going to head back home, I’ve got so many calls to make, so many people to check up on that I couldn’t get through to earlier. Ooh, is that a new vase? I love it. Where did you get? And the flowers are beautiful too. Wow, they're fake, they look so real. I want some. You have got such amazing taste. I love it, love it, love it. Actually tell me later, I should get out of your hair. So much to do. Goodbye my lovelies.’
She gave Amy a huge hug and came over to me to administer mine.
’Be Well’ she whispered, ensuring it was out of Amy’s earshot.
She had noticed it too. I was now even more intrigued to discuss the speech with her.
‘Do come back later for a glass of wine if you like’ I offered. Perhaps the ‘do’ was more of an insistence than an offer.
Amy is in the kitchen, making phone calls to her parents, brothers and assorted friends. I’m leaving her to it.

I’m slouched on the sofa. In my TV watching spot. Except there’s no TV to watch. I try to send a few texts, all of a fairly prosaic nature. I’ve no idea if they’ll get through. I try to call mum a few times. It doesn't connect. Networks overloaded with millions of people doing the same. It’s like the 90’s. The good old days. No video calls, WhatsApp or email.

I try to recall parts of the speech that stood out. News channel analysis and social media commentary noticeable by their absence. No memes. No conspiracies. Just peace, space, solitude. A chance to gather my thoughts. Emphasis on my. No algorithm to steer, guide, distract or divert.

‘Your savings are safe.’ That line that got me. ‘Your deposits are protected. Nothing has been lost — only temporarily made inaccessible’. How many people were immediately concerned about their savings? I’m pretty sure most people would have been wondering when they could next buy a skinny latte or a meal deal. If they will be able to do the weekly shop tomorrow. When Google and Netflix will be back online. Not concern their savings account. Well, not until the point it was mentioned, anyway. The fact this was even referenced so soon after the 'attack' is, well, interesting.

The change in tone towards the end. Dark and challenging days ahead. Really? The PM left us hanging with this. The initial reassurance and composure became hints at unnamed issues we’d be facing. Thinking back, it’s odd that no one picked up on this. I’d really like to see it again. Surely there’ll be replays? In fact I’m surprised it’s not on a permanent loop on BBC. Do they not want it scrutinised? I should’ve recorded it on my phone.
I must make sure I video the next one in the morning.

And of course there was the sign off. How many hours of behavioural psychology went into the creation of those two words? Be Well. It’s not Goodnight. Nor is it Stay Safe or God Bless. It's a directive disguised as a farewell. It tells you what to be. It assumes the authority to instruct your emotional state. Kate will know more. I hope she comes back for a glass of wine. A psychologist trained to see the structure of the speech. She’d separate the intent from the content.
Dev will have clocked that two word sign off too. And plenty more aside. I should text him. Be Well. Maybe an eyebrow raised emoji too? No, scrap the emoji. Dev wouldn't send one.

I wish he were here. We’d spend the night breaking the address down, analysing the structure, the implications, trying to predict the timeline from here. He’d somehow stay coherent after multiple bottles of red and a half-empty bottle of whiskey.
But he’s not here.

The shops being shut today didn’t impact us. In addition to the cannellini bean stockpile, we’d done a big shop on Saturday before Valentine’s Day. Lots of root veg, pulses, stock and stewing cut of meat - scrag end of lamb, pork shoulder, beef short ribs, cheek and oxtail.
We decided to cook the lamb tonight - pressure cooked with carrots, leeks, onions, stock white wine, pearl barley, rosemary and bay leaves. One potful of traditional, rustic, hearty nourishment.

The five of us ate at the dining table, the small log burner in the kitchen roaring, dogs huddled up on their bed in the corner, no doubt desperate for us to drink enough wine that we’d waive our no scraps from the table policy. I decided to play some vinyl - educate the kids in a classic - an album that told a tale.
I held up the album cover before removing the vinyl from its gatefold sleeve - Marvin Gaye’s What’s Going On. 180g limited edition. An excellent choice if I say so myself.
‘Recommended for You’ I said with a wink. Surely one of them will get my nod to Spotify?
I resisted the urge to sing along and ruin it. The title track. So apt. Three minutes fifty-one seconds of perfection.
You know we've got to find a way, to bring some loving here today.

None of the kids had heard the album before. They hadn’t even heard of Marvin Gaye. They seemed to dig it though. How could anyone not dig it? I’ve no idea why I’ve used the term dig it. A bit of Marvin on the turntable and I suddenly think I’m John Shaft.

Annoyingly, Mercy Mercy Me (my favourite song on the album) was interrupted by the scheduled 9pm Emergency Alert klaxon - five phones screeching - two dogs barking. Some shops and pharmacies will open tomorrow, limited hours, cash only.
They’re not going to do essential retail again, aren’t they?
Emilia pointed out the obvious flaw with the ‘Remain at Home’ part of the message. ‘How can we stay at home and go to the shops?’
No one commented on the military and police part, so I didn’t either. ‘To help with co-ordination’, eh? I wonder what’s been happening on the streets that we’re not being told?

The album finished. I toy with the idea of another one but everyone seems tired, still a bit hungover (we’d had a couple of glasses of red wine hair of the dog) and just a little shellshocked. We decide an early night’s in order. The kids head for their rooms. Amy loads the dishwasher. I toy with the idea of a bourbon - there’s a bottle of  Eagle Rare calling me from the drinks cabinet - but I think better of it.
A spate of texts come through just before ten. Sarah, to let me know that Sam’s back. Mum, to tell me that ‘Tony has sorted everything’, whatever the fuck that means. And Dev? Nothing from Dev yet.

A 10pm Emergency ‘Overnight Update’ reassures us that there are ‘no threats to security’ and gives us a little goodnight peck on the cheek - ‘Sleep Safely’. Did we really need a klaxon going off to tell us this? I can feel the pain of parents with young babies around the country, children needlessly awoken to tell them to sleep safely. On the bright side the klaxon gave me a timely reminder to take my ‘night time’ insulin - 38 units of Lantus long acting basal insulin, taken at ten o’clock, or as near as damn it, every evening.

Tucked up in bed, before half-ten. How civilised. The dogs have had their wees - they weren’t keen to go out in the freezing sleet, but Amy made them. The bedroom is cold - we had the central heating on in here earlier but it became way too hot and stuffy, so we opened the window, and now it’s bloody freezing. We’ve got extra blankets. I’m half tempted to make a hot water bottle. Rock and fucking roll, baby.
Ten-thirty, here comes ARC Emergency with its snazzy teal and dulcet notification tone.
This is the embodiment of ‘Be Well’. Was that a one-off sign-off or will it become a thing? My money is on the latter.
Apparently we can now receive verified local updates by ‘enabling notifications’. The ‘opt-in’ for an app that auto-installed without consent. Hilarious.
‘Should I enable notifications?’ Amy asks.

‘Why not? What difference will it make? The app has already downloaded itself. Automatically.’ I reply, flicking through the Settings menu. ‘It’s obviously going to be useful to know what’s actually open’.
‘Is this right?’ Amy shows me her screen.
‘Yeah, I think so. Same thing I’ve done.’

I click on the ARC app to see if anything has changed. Nothing. The app doesn’t seem to have any functionality other than receiving messages. It doesn’t open like a normal app. I hold my finger on it to see if there are any options. Still nothing. Not even the option to delete it.
‘Text from Kate’ Amy breaks my thought process about the un-deletable app. ‘She’s knackered, not coming. Might come over for the morning briefing.’

‘This is going to become a thing isn’t it?’ I imply that having a neighbour over for every broadcast (however many every turns out to be) might become a little intrusive, but really I feel that watching nudge unit output with a psychologist is a big win. ‘Tell her I’ll have a pot of tea ready for nine.’
That’ll make sure she comes. A pot of tea is a more solid offer than a cup.
‘Right, last message. I want to read now.’ Amy announces.

I consider bringing up the subject of the markets this week. Will we be able to open? How will we contact the traders? So many questions, but no answers at this stage. We’ve just got to wait and see how the week progresses. I decide to keep quiet. The right choice.

Amy puts down her phone and starts to read. She always reads before bed. I toy with the idea of reading too. The final few chapters of Freedom are calling me, but I’m too tired to respond. I know I should. No excuse. No distractions. The quiet is total — no background hum of the internet, no notifications, no feed to doomscroll. No memes, no tweets, no articles, no commentary.
I feel my mind start trying to piece it all together. The military manoeuvres. The heightened cyber attack threats. The gematria. The biometric OTA push. Dev warned, Dev knew. It’s coming…
Stop. Stop it. Sleep. Now. Whilst you’re tired, whilst you can.

I wake up. My hand habitually reaches out for my phone. The first check. The time. Crikey, 8.07. A lie in. I chuckle to myself at the irony of getting a proper night’s sleep the day after The Event. No 3am wake up. No middle of the night research. I didn't even get up for a wee. A blissful nine hours of unbroken sleep. Blood sugar check - 7.1 - good. I turn my head to see if Amy is still in bed. She is. Fast asleep. Did she not set her alarm? I try to open X. Email. BBC homepage. Still nothing.

I head to the toilet for a much needed wee. Several UK Gov and ARC messages. One at 6am. Did the klaxon not go off? Or did I sleep through it? I scroll through the messages. Emergency Red vs Reassuring Teal. No significant updates it seems. Something from ARC Local - Boots and Waitrose are open. Cash payments only. Good job I didn't listen to Dev on this.
Morning wee finished. Time for a cup of tea.

It turns out that the difficult second cup lived up to its name today. It wasn’t just a cup. It was a pot. Two pots in fact. One of Earl Grey for Amy. One of normal tea for Kate and me. A tray. A jug of milk. A bowl of sugar. Teaspoons. Cups and saucers. A plate of warm almond croissants that Kate brought over sits on the side table. Very civilised.

It’s five to nine, just the three of us seated on the sofa waiting for the BBC broadcast. The kids are still in bed. Amy and I debated whether to wake them up or let them lie in. We opted for the latter.
Here it comes… Listen with Auntie…

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — PM ADDRESS — 09:00 GMT — 16 FEBRUARY 2027
turns.title: PM Address · Day 2 Morning

paras.t: ‘Over to you, Kate. Break it down for us.’ I put an imaginary microphone up to her mouth.

She smiles, tears off a piece of croissant and pops it in her mouth. She holds her finger up to buy herself some time. She's thinking. I can see her composing something — choosing where to start. She lands on an easy target first.
'The thanking.
Did you hear the thanking?
We followed the guidance - the country has had a calm and orderly night - he thanked us.
That's a reward.
You behaved.
Good. Now here's the next instruction. It's a pattern you use with —'
She catches herself. Professional boundary. She was about to say ‘patients’ or ‘clients?’

'It's a compliance loop. Acknowledge the behaviour you want repeated, then immediately set the next task. Don't leave a gap for people to question whether they want to keep complying. You just tell them they already are, and move on.’

‘God I wish she'd been on the sofa with us during Boris and his cronies Covid addresses. She knows her stuff. Our personal behavioural insight analyst.’ I interrupt her flow with a compliment delivered by addressing Amy.
'I'm not sure you and Dev needed much help. Every speech, every utterance picked apart for hidden meaning for hours on end.’ Amy recalls the endless analysis with something other than fondness.
Kate picks up her tea. Sips. She’s watching Amy now, not me.

'The other thing. Last night he said days, not weeks. This morning he said it again. Identical phrase. That's not someone updating us — that's someone reinforcing an anchor. If the timeline had changed, he'd use different words. The fact he's repeating the exact phrase means it's not information. It's a mantra.'
‘Ah, the return of the mantra. The affirmation. Hypnosis. Voodoo.’ I pretend to dangle a pendant on a chain in front of her eyes.

‘Look into my eyes, look into my eyes, the eyes, the eyes, not around the eyes, don't look around my eyes, look into my eyes, you're under.’ Amy continues to lighten the mood with a passable Kenny from Little Britain impression.
‘Tell me more Kate.' I inadvertently sit forward on the edge of the sofa, I'm fully engaged, ready to dive deeper into behavioural science analysis with a pro.
'Covid gave us three part chunking - Stay Home, Protect the NHS, Save Lives - that was good. They got sloppy though - what was it? Stay Alert and Control the Virus - ludicrous.’
Kate's eyes light up. This is seemingly her thing.
'Oh God, don't get me started. OK, quickly.’
She puts her tea down and counts on her fingers to highlight her point.

‘Stay Home, Protect the NHS, Save Lives. That was beautiful. Three beats. Action, altruism, outcome. You know exactly what to do and you feel good about doing it. Seventy-seven per cent spontaneous awareness within days — that's unheard of for a government message. Most public health campaigns would kill for thirty.’
She's animated now.

'Then they got cocky. Stay Alert, Control the Virus, Save Lives. Same three-beat structure but the first clause was changed from an instruction to a... vibe. Stay alert? Alert to what? How? You've gone from do this thing to be this way. And the public felt it immediately — it was mocked within hours. Because it reintroduced ambiguity, and ambiguity is the enemy of compliance.’
She reaches for her tea again, catches herself mid-reach and keeps going.

'Then Hands, Face, Space. No verbs at all. Pure compression. Three nouns. Practically a mantra at that point. And when the third lockdown came, what did they do? Went straight back to the original. Stay Home, Protect the NHS, Save Lives. Unchanged. Because the first one worked and every iteration since was far worse.’
She picks up the tea. Takes a small sip.
'The lesson they learned — and this is the thing — is that specificity beats abstraction every time. Tell people what to do, not how to feel.’
She pauses. Looks at the TV. Amy and I unconsciously look at it too. The BBC holding card is still there.

'Which is why this morning is interesting. Because he's not doing that. He hasn't given us a slogan. Last night he had three requests — stay local, don't fear, follow ARC. Three beats. But it's not compressed. It's not a bumper sticker. The only thing that sticks is two words at the end.’
She pauses.
‘Be Well.’ Amy replies. Slowly, deliberately, mockingly. She’d noticed it too. We hadn’t talked about it.
‘Be Well’ Kate repeats. ’That’s not Stay Home, Protect the NHS, Save Lives. It's not an instruction. It's not even three parts. It's two words that tell you what to be.

‘And it worked on all of us immediately.’ I note with a wry smile. ‘And also, did you notice something else in the emergency alert — the klaxon one, not the speech. Stay Home. Stay Calm. Two parts. The third instruction noticeable by its absence.’
Kate looks at me. Not the way she looked at Amy — that was checking for fragility. This is something else. Reassessment.
'You counted the beats.'
It's not a question.
'You sat there last night, during the klaxon, and you counted the beats.’
She puts her cup down. The careful placement again.
'So here's what's interesting about that. Stay Home, Stay Calm — two parts.
She glances at Amy.

'The klaxon — Stay Home. Stay Calm. Two beats. Everyone who lived through Covid is conditioned to expect three. The rhythm is incomplete. And an incomplete rhythm does one of two things — it either feels like a mistake, which makes you distrust the source, or it creates an open loop. Your brain wants to close it. It keeps searching for the third instruction. Which means you're still listening. You're not satisfied. You haven't filed it away and moved on. You're waiting.'
She glances at the TV. So do I. So does Amy.

'And then the PM comes on. I ask three things of you. First. Second. Third. The loop closes. The relief is unconscious but it's real. The klaxon opened a gap. The speech filled it. This is not something that happened accidentally.'
She picks up the croissant again. A smaller piece this time. A nibble. Almost absent-mindedly.

'The question I keep asking myself is — who's writing this? Not the PM. He's delivering it. But this is authored. The alert and the address are two halves of one piece of communication. The gap was designed. The resolution was designed. Someone is structuring the sequence, not just the individual messages.’

I’m still sitting on the edge of the sofa. Leaning in. Engrossed. ‘So many questions. Who is writing the sequence? When was it written? Presumably it was written by a committee at a cyber-security convention? Just in case there happens to be a cyber attack. And the next parts of the sequence - the ARC messages last night and this morning? The ARC Local stuff - an app that auto-installed itself and can’t be deleted is suddenly asking us to grant it permission. And the rest of the speech this morning. He thanked us, what did he say after that? Remember I’ve got it filmed on my phone if we need to see it again.’
‘He’s a proper little detective, isn’t he?’ Amy says, a mixture of commitment and mockery.
Kate ignores Amy's detective comment. Not rudely — she just doesn't register it. She's locked on to one of the questions I asked.
'The ARC thing. An app installs itself on your phone. You didn't download it. You didn't agree to it. You didn't even know it was happening. And then — then — it asks you to enable notifications.’
I thought this was the one she’d focus on.
‘Would you like to opt in? As if you have a choice. The app that appeared on your phone uninvited is now politely knocking on the door it already walked through.’
She looks at Amy.
'Did you enable notifications last night?'
‘Yes.'
'Did it feel like a decision?’
‘Um, yeah, I guess so?’

'It wasn't. The decision was made when the app installed. Everything after that is theatre. But it's important theatre — because you need to feel like you chose. If they'd just pushed notifications without asking, you'd feel surveilled. Instead they asked, and you said yes, and now it's yours. You opted in. It's consensual. Except the thing you consented to was already running.’
She turns to me.

'It's the same technique as the savings line last night. "Your savings are safe." Nobody was worried about their savings until he said it. He introduced the anxiety and resolved it in the same sentence. You feel reassured about something you weren't concerned about — which means you're now grateful for information you didn't ask for, from a source you didn't choose. That's not reassurance. That's a dependency loop. He's training you to need him.’

‘To need him and to need the app’ I reply. ‘I wonder how many people enabled it? I did, because, well, why not. And I’m the sort of person that wouldn’t enable it, as a matter of principle. Because I’m…the suspicious sort. Without the emergency, without the need, with alternative influencers screaming privacy and psyop, I wonder how many would have voluntarily downloaded it or enabled permissions? But we need to know which shops are open. An unambiguous requirement. What was it you said? Ambiguity is the enemy of compliance?’
Kate doesn't reply immediately. She's looking at me differently now. Not reassessment this time, but recognition.

'That's exactly it. You've just described the most effective persuasion architecture there is. You don't overcome resistance. You make resistance irrelevant. Give people a reason they can't argue with — which shops are open, where the nearest pharmacy is — and the thing they'd never voluntarily accept becomes the thing they need. The container doesn't matter anymore. Nobody's thinking about the container. They're thinking about the paracetamol.'
She picks up her tea. It must be nearly cold by now.

'I could have every objection in the world to that app. But if my client is in crisis and the only way I can find out whether the surgery is open is through ARC Local — I'm enabling notifications. And I'm not even angry about it. I'm grateful.'
Amy puts her mug down. Not Kate's careful placement —this is I-mean-business placement.
'Can I say something?’
It's not like Amy to ask permission to speak. Kate and I both notice.

'This cyber attack. People had been predicting it. For weeks. Months. Not just the conspiracy realists (she winks at me, noting that she’s using one of my terms)  — mainstream journalists, security people. I wasn't paying attention at the time but Simon was, and I was half-listening, the way you do.'
She's not looking at either of us. She's looking at the ARC icon on her phone, on the coffee table.

'And this response. It doesn't look like something they threw together on Saturday night. The app looks slick. A logo. A colour scheme. The messages are worded like they've been through fifteen drafts. The PM’s script is polished. Refined. Community hubs are opening today — today — with printed signage and designated locations in every local authority. That doesn't happen in thirty-six hours. It’s a plan being activated.’
She pauses.
'So either they're incredibly well prepared for something they said wouldn't happen. Or they knew it would.'

She’s asking all the right questions. Well, some of them anyway. Amy knows what I’ll think. She’s laid this out for Kate to reply to even though it was notionally aimed at both of us. I keep quiet and wait for Kate to step in.
She takes a moment.

'I don't think those two things are as separate as you'd think. Prepared for something they said wouldn't happen — that's literally my job. I have crisis plans for clients I hope will never need them. Hospitals have major incident protocols they rehearse every year. Being prepared doesn't mean you caused it.'
She stops. I can see a but coming. The words that follow the but will show how awake Kate is. I genuinely don't know. We’ve never gone here before.
‘But.'
She looks at the ARC icon on Amy's phone. The same place Amy was looking.

'But there's a difference between having a plan in a drawer and having an app with a logo on forty million phones within twelve hours. There's a difference between a crisis protocol and a communications sequence that's been psychologically optimised for compliance before the crisis is two days old. One is preparedness. The other is…'
I wait for her to finish the sentence. She doesn't. It’s Amy who breaks.
‘Anyone want another tea? I’m going to make one for the kids. It’s time they got up.’
The other is…what Kate? Say the words…
‘I’m going to head back next door. I’m going to look into the local community hub, see if they need any volunteers.’
Very noble. Exactly the thing I should do but won’t.
‘Let us know what you find out. You sure you don’t want another cup?’ Amy asks.
‘No, I’m tea-ed out. Maybe see you later for the next one?’
‘Three times a week is a habit.’ I smile as I point out.
‘Oh, Tranquility by Tuesday. Laura Vanderkam. Have you read it?’
I hadn’t. I just knew the quote.
‘No, I haven’t.’
‘I’ll lend it to you. Worth a read. See you at six!’
Amy blows her a kiss.
She sends one back as she departs, accompanying it with a merry little wave. The words Be Well form on the tip of my tongue. I resist the urge to speak them.
The six of us convene around the kitchen table a little after ten. Eight of us if you include the dogs, who pace ceaselessly round and round the table, sock in mouth.
‘Go to your bed, dog’ Chloe shouts grumpily, suddenly realising what it is that’s annoying her.
Six cups of tea (builders for the boys, Earl Grey for Amy and Emilia and a herbal infusion for Chloe). I’m not sure what it is. It’s deep red though. A berry of some sort.

‘Shall we make a plan then’ suggests Amy as she puts a selection of spreadables on the table — butter, Marmite, honey from the local apiary and an unlabelled jar of jam — rhubarb and ginger I believe.
We look at one another, nodding in agreement that a plan should be made, but no one suggesting what it might be.

George breaks the silence. ‘So to recap, stay home, stay local. Help your neighbours. Go to a community hub if you need to. Retail is closed. Or is that non-essential businesses are closed. But now there’s a designated network of shops that are open. Which according to ARC Local are all the supermarkets in town.’
‘Toast’s up’ — Amy puts the first six slices on the table and within a split second each child has one on their plate.
‘Right. Let’s all head into town. See what’s open. We do need a few bits.’
‘Milk’ — Amy starts the list.
‘I need some more chamomile tea.’ Chloe adds.
‘Day Two of The Cyber Attack and Chloe needs herbal tea’ says Sam, in a mocking American movie trailer accent.
Giggles all round, other than from Chloe who gives her stepbrother that stare.
‘Have you girls got schoolwork to do?’
Now it’s my turn to get that stare, this time from both girls.
‘Well, kind of, yeah. But, like, whatever.’ Says Emilia, a reply that looks even worse in writing than it sounded.
‘OK, let’s leave at eleven. Drive in, check out the lie of the land, buy milk and herbal tea, come back, take the dogs for a walk, and then just wait, I guess? See what update we get at six.’
‘Take cash’ Amy reminds me.
I dutifully head off to raid the piggy bank.

It’s only a five minute drive into town. There are a fair few cars on the road. Testament to the rather unclear advice about what constitutes an ‘essential journey’ — especially as ‘essential retail’ is open. A sign that people aren’t falling into line quite as quickly as they did with Covid? Once bitten?
‘What’s for dinner, Pa?’ Sam asks from the middle seat (left hand side, he’s had a weird superstition about that seat since he was a toddler).
‘Beef stew of some sort’ I reply.
‘Beef Bourguignon?’ he asks, pleadingly.
‘I’m not sure we have any mushrooms or shallots’
‘We can get some?’
‘OK. We’ll need a cheap bottle of Pinot Noir too.’
