I’d imagined the fallout from a cyber attack on many occasions. Apocalyptic. No power. Mad Max chaos. Never a family trip to Waitrose discussing our winter menu.
‘Jesus, look at the queue’ cries Emilia from the back seat.

The queue to the car park trails back about a quarter of a mile. It’s monitored by a handful of Sussex policemen (and one policewoman), twice as many Community Support Officers, several Security Guards and a pathos-inducing octogenarian Lollipop Man, who, bless him, seems as much use as a chocolate teapot.

No military presence here. They’ve been reserved for less well-heeled parts of Sussex no doubt. The queuing system is orderly, considerate. Very English. Spirits are high. A slightly coy, self-conscious and reserved Blitz spirit.
We decide to turn around, park on the outskirts of town and walk in.
When we arrive at Waitrose, the queue to get in is just as monstrous.
‘I wonder if there’s a one way system in operation in store’ I say, laughing maniacally. ‘You can still see the 2m distance footprints in some aisles. I wonder if they’ll decommission them?’
‘This is ridiculous.’ Chloe speaks for all of us.

‘Agreed. We’ve got enough food to last us a good few weeks if the shit hits the fan. I’m not queuing up for two hours to buy milk and a few odds and ends. We can have black coffee or herbal tea. Slum it.’

‘Dev was certain there’s no need to stock up, no need to hoard cash. I mean, he’s clearly not totally right in the short term. But if it’s just a few days as predicted, all this crazy queuing will be a complete waste of time.’
‘So you now believe the official line, do you? Days, not weeks.’ Asks George.

‘I didn’t say that. But the most likely scenario is that there has been a cyber attack of some sort. An actual one, a false flag? Who knows? Either way, the effect is the same. Payment systems are down. Everyone’s panicking. Amazing the number of people that can remember how to use cash when they need to, isn’t it?’
I stop myself before a rant develops. ‘Let’s go back. Walk the dogs?’
We’re about to turn and head back to the car.
‘Let’s go back the High Street way, see what’s open’ suggests Amy.

There are a few shops open. Those that decided to self-identify as ‘essential’. The butcher, the greengrocer, the Italian cheese and wine shop. The barbers. It’s all rather buzzy and convivial. Far busier than your average Tuesday morning.
‘Look’ — George points at the pub on the corner. ‘They are opening up.’ A chalkboard is placed on the pavement outside the front doors.
£5 A PINT UNTIL 6PM — CASH ONLY
‘Must be selling scotch eggs’ I quip. The joke may have gone over the kids’ heads, but not Amy’s. She gives me a playful pat on the bum.
‘There’s a Community Hub I’d be happy to pay a visit to.’ Amy smiles, raising an eyebrow.
‘It’s not even midday yet guys’ Emilia interjects in the manner of a Victorian Aunt.
She’s right though. We waited until lunchtime during the Plandemic. Most days anyway.
We head back to the car, somewhat reluctantly, memories of all-day sessions at Uni hitting hard.
‘Where is the actual Community Hub by the way?’ I ask Amy.
‘I don’t actually know. If it’s at the Community Centre it’s up the other end of the High Street I think.’ She replies.
Neither of us actually know. We’d have known where to find the shallots in Waitrose though. I feel a pang of something that’s quite possibly guilt. I ignore it.

The walk with the dogs was really rather lovely. We went to the woods just after lunch (chicken soup). The air was clean, crisp and pine-scented. We don’t often all go out for a walk together anymore. Not like we used to in the old days. Like I see on the photos ‘Memories’ montages my phone packages and presents to me without my prompting. ‘Devon 2015’ or ‘In The Ashdown Forest Over the Years’.
Memories. Bittersweet. Come on, hold it together.
Not having internet on the phones was refreshing. Not that there’s much phone reception in the woods anyway. But just the knowledge that most of the smartphone functions were disabled was liberating.
Things were better before they introduced these bastard things.
I’d only taken mine as the continuous blood glucose monitoring app on it has become a bit of a crutch. I’ve no idea how I used to cope without it.

I had a dozen or so voice messages and numerous texts from market traders when service returned. I’d changed the voicemail message this morning to say that we didn’t know if the markets would be running this week and we’d advise in due course. Yet still they left messages asking if we’d open. I know their livelihood depends upon it. So does ours. Having seen the open shops this morning I was confident we’d be able to open. Communicating that without email and WhatsApp group messages was going to be tricky though.
I should change the voicemail message again, say we are definitely open. Or should I wait for permission from the council? Fuck knows.
Anyway, I’m here in the kitchen with the boys. I’m starting on the beef stew — stout and turnips replacing the red wine and mushrooms of the Bourguignon. Hearty peasant grub.

We’ve been chewing the fat for a bit. I’ve been skirting around any deep chat. Any predictions. Any dot connecting. I don’t know why. It’s unlike me. Maybe I just want to see how it plays out. The questions verging on the mundane. Will Sam still be able to do his six weeks in Australia next month? Will there be Premier League games this weekend? When will the internet be back up and running? George pointed out that this shutdown will cost him money every day.

My view is that they probably have taken the internet down purely as a precaution — or at least the pretence of a precaution — rather than it being hacked. Either way it’s not working. My hunch is it’ll be back in days. There will be uproar without it. Half the country would rather starve than be without their precious TikTok.

All they have at the moment is the telly with the PM address on loop when he’s not presenting live interspersed with ARC Emergency ‘Situation Update’ scrolling across the screen like a non-interactive social media-lite.

Amy comes into the kitchen again. She’s been in and out for the last hour or so. Never settling. Laps of the house from kitchen to bathroom to utility room and back again. Stoking the fire in the hallway. Doing the bits and bobs that keep the ship afloat.
‘Right, fuck this’ she announces as she takes a seat on a stool at the island. ‘Let’s have some wine.’
I duly oblige by opening a bottle of red. A German Pinot Noir. Too good to make a stew with.
‘Four glasses?’ I ask. George answers in the affirmative immediately. Sam, far less bothered by booze, decides he might as well have one too.
‘OK, what the bloody hell is going on? Simon, you never stop predicting this sort of thing. Here it is, and you’re so quiet about it. I don’t know, you seem slightly detached. Kind of smug.

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — JOINT ADDRESS — 18:00 GMT — 16 FEBRUARY 2027
turns.title: Joint Address · Day 2 Evening

paras.t: Days of the week have a certain feel. Everyone knows this. Friday has a spring in its step. Sunday evening carries a low-grade existential dread that no amount of roast potato can fully neutralise. Monday is Monday. Wednesday is the day nobody has ever written a song about. Actually ‘a boring Wednesday’ is referenced in That’s Entertainment, I take it back. Even the weird no-man's-land between Christmas and New Year has a feel — the feel of a screensaver put on the laptop of your life while it waits for further instructions.

Today didn't feel like any of them. It felt, well, just different. Not the different I might have expected. It felt muted. Flat. Redolent of the Come on, do something cartoon meme where the man prods something with a stick. In this case a cyber attack.

A cyber attack that has been brewing. At least another event of magnitude has. Another pandemic ‘that really gets our attention’. Or some sort of hybrid clusterfuck. What was it branded by WEF? A polycrisis I believe? Something Big has always been just around the corner. I’ve been waiting for it the way a storm chaser waits for a tornado. Years of tracking, predicting, preparing, being dismissed. And now it's here. And it’s a little anti-climactic.

I’m not going to lie, when the klaxon went off it was exhilarating. I’d never felt more alive. Every nerve started firing. The internet - down, payment systems - not operating, people - confused, scared. I was buzzing. This was vindication.
This was I fucking told you so.

But now, two days in, the I fucking told you so has become Kate with a Victoria sponge cake in front of The Beeb instead of an angry mob with pitch forks in front of The Houses of Parliament. I’d expected Mad Max and so far we’ve had a long weekend with beef stew and dog walks.
It’s confusing AND suspicious AND — if I’m honest — disappointing? Not that I wanted chaos. Well not total chaos. But enough to liven all you stiffs up a bit, to paraphrase Withnail.
The gap between Schwab's ‘it will make COVID seem like a small disturbance’ and the actual experience - deciding not to queue at Waitrose for shallots - is a gap I’m yet to get to grips with.
Perhaps the flatness IS the design. A crisis calibrated to be just severe enough to justify the response and just mild enough that nobody panics.

In fact, the household tonight is the very opposite of a state of panic. There was very little discussion at the end of the broadcast. Some shoulder shrugs, some mutterings of ‘back to normal soon, it seems’ and sighs of relief that the internet would soon be back up and running. ‘Reassuring’ offered George, and he appeared to speak for all the kids. Kate had given us a quick lowdown on the community hub - in short - tea, cake and gossip and had left with a ‘might see you tomorrow?’ rather than a definite same time, same place for the next instalment.

We’re well fed (the stew hit the spot, every last drop demolished - and I’d cooked enough to feed a dozen), pleasantly tired from the walk, fresh winter air and a few glasses of red, and well, content. The children are in their rooms - offline gaming for the boys, gossip and giggles from the girls. Amy headed to bed to read just before ten.
Me? I’m sitting at the kitchen table, mulling things over, glass of bourbon in hand. Eagle Rare 10 Year Old.
I’ve tried calling Dev quite a few times. Nothing. Not connecting to voicemail, not ringing. Just nothing. I’ve texted him too. No idea if he’s receiving them.

So it’s just me sitting with my own thoughts. The peace occasionally punctuated by a crackle from the dying embers of the fire. Solitude. Other than the dogs, curled up contentedly by my feet. I doubt they’re analysing the PM’s words. Well, perhaps Olive.

I must admit there was something reassuring about the words of the PM and his cohorts tonight. Their performance suggested normality was imminent. Of course there will be repercussions, fast-tracked regulations and vows that ‘we will do everything within our power to ensure this doesn't happen again’. But ultimately it’s a blip that will be ironed out with the appropriate solutions.

I pick up my phone. It’s become a 1999 Nokia in function. And I kind of like it. At the same time I really want to be able to scroll my way through the X algo. Or dive into some juicy cyber attack Substacks. All I’ve got is a selection of ‘how’s it going?’ texts from friends and family and Arc Emergency - which has been updated with the transcript of the 6pm Joint Address. I give it a read.
The key words, the morale boosters - Orderly - Calm - Patient - Normal - Broadly Positive - On Schedule

Our introduction to a new sidekick on the podium - Paul Chichester from The National Cyber Security Centre. Jargon Man. He’s the cyber attack’s Chris Whitty - replacing Covid’s atypical pneumonia, consensus sequence, r0, Case Fatality Rate, etc with cyber-tech jargon. Jargon that sounds plausible but that most people won’t be able to fully comprehend, let alone challenge. Stay in your lane, good people. Trust the experts.

Apparently - ‘The attack targeted the legacy public-key cryptography that has underpinned online banking and card payments for thirty years — the algorithms RSA, ECDSA, Diffie-Hellman. These standards have now been comprehensively compromised across the twenty-three affected nations.’
Dev could explain this. I can picture him giving a real-time running commentary. Not only translating the jargon but explaining the architecture behind the words.
Also I note it was - ‘designed to undermine trust in the cryptography, not to encrypt or to steal.’
Cui bono? Sorry, rhetorical question. Who, or what, always benefits? And if trust is lost, what do you do? Rebuild it. Stronger than before. More resilient. Better.
This is also intriguing - ‘ARC operates at the device level, beneath the application layer, and uses post-quantum cryptographic standards. It has not been compromised by this attack.’
They’re bringing back the layer that has been compromised. Whilst the biometrics functions from the OTA push sit dormant.
And of course there’s - ‘Good night. And Be Well.’

Be Well. The third time he's said it. Slightly affected, slightly knowing, said in a manner that you had to notice, but that simultaneously comes across as a pleasantry. A caring sign-off. The verbal equivalent of a wave. Kate heard it on night one. Whispered it back to me like a question she already knew the answer to.

The same two words, in the same cadence, at the end of every address. As a one off sign off it was worthy of a Roger Moore eyebrow raise. But three times? Nobody writes the same sign-off three times by accident. Someone chose those words. Designed them. Tested them.

‘Be Well.’ Not ‘Stay Safe.’ That was Covid, that was Boris, that was fear dressed as concern during those early lockdown days — March 2020, the sun, the empty roads, the daily countryside walks, the family together, Amy's sourdough phase, the kids doing school on Zoom in their pyjamas, bumbled briefings, raging at the telly. The guilty pleasure of furlough. The Scamdemic apocalypse was the best family holiday I'd ever had.
Take the rose tinted spectacles off, you prick.
Where was I? Ah yes, ‘Be Well.’

’Be Well’ is warmer. Paternal. The government wishing us wellness, not warning us of danger. A blessing, almost. But with the undertone that not Being Well is not an option. Am I reading too much into two words? Probably.

Sign off aside, the Prime Minister was convincing tonight. That's the thing. He didn’t appear to be lying. He spoke the language of institutions. Of competence. Of managed outcomes. The language that says: we have this. The language understood by those who haven’t bothered to ask ‘who designed the we.'
He delivered it well.
‘I trust you to handle the truth, and I have given you as much of it as we have.’
But he was omitting.

I witnessed a man who knew much more than he was letting on, more than he was at liberty to say - more than his script allowed. Did he know the full picture? I doubt it. How many do? The full picture is compartmentalised. It exists in a place he doesn't have access to. It’s above his pay grade.

But he knows the direction of travel. You’d have to have your head lodged firmly up your arse not to. One doesn't need the full picture to know that the reassuring, not too cold, not too hot script is a lie by omission.

Exhibit A: The firmware analysis. The one Dev sent me on Signal. It’s still there on my phone. An undocumented OTA push. Undocumented is doing some work here, considering the fact that it’s here. Documented. Also analysed by a not-suspicious-at-all, newly-created anonymous systems analyst Substack account. And debunked (yet simultaneously amplified) by multiple mainstream media outlets.
I open my phone with Face ID (yeah, I know) and find the analysis Dev sent. Documents like this don’t just happen. They aren’t accidentally pre-positioned.

I read it again, slowly. A dormant service container provisioned with local storage permissions, NFC write access, and an encrypted callback to a routing address that resolves to BIS infrastructure in Basel.
My mind turns to the firmware analysis Substack. It’s not saved to my phone, so I can’t access it, but the last few lines are inked into my memory.
It is not active. It is waiting. I don’t know what it’s waiting for.

I bet he’s closer to knowing now. But if he’s like me he’ll be closer, but not there yet. The thing that survived is the thing that was pre-positioned. The thing being restored is the thing that was attacked. The dormant biometric layer sits there, untouched, waiting. The cognitive dissonance between the severity of the prediction and the banality of the experience is…what?
A data point? Worthy of note? Confusing as fuck? I don't know how to read it yet. Broadly speaking it’s surely either one of two scenarios.

Here they are - the absence of any external analysis or algorithmic distractions has given me time to craft something a little more considered than trying to cram some analysis into a two hundred and eighty character maximum tweet. (My account isn’t verified - what a rebel, eh? A real body blow to the system)

The first scenario, the tiptoe. The event is contained. Multiple nations, including many of the likely suspects. Global payment systems frozen. Internet, the public facing elements at least, suspended. But no cascading effects. Yet. The attack is real but manageable. The communication blackout will lift within days, payment systems will come back online within a week or two. Life will resume. But — and this is the mechanism — the legislation that will follow will be permanent. Emergency powers that will become structural. The Patriot Act model: a contained crisis producing permanent architecture. The event doesn't need to be catastrophic. It needs to be sufficient. Sufficient to justify Digital ID. Sufficient to justify centralised payment infrastructure. Sufficient to make ‘we can't let this happen again’ the unassailable political position. The crisis as pretext for pre-written legislation that was sitting in policy papers years before the crisis existed.

The second scenario, the polycrisis cometh. We’re currently fighting our way through level one, easy mode, yet to reach the end of level guardian. In fact we’re probably still in the tutorial. This Victoria Sponge Crisis is just the amuse-fucking-bouche. The communication blackout isn't a side effect of the attack — it's the attack's primary function. Sever horizontal communication, establish an official channel as the single source of truth, and then deliver the next blow while we’re isolated and informed only by the people who are managing the crisis. The Davos polycrisis - a cascading, compounding series of interconnected shocks. A series of end of level guardians - cyber, then energy, then supply chain, then public health. Each one justifying the next escalation. Each escalation making the previous emergency powers look proportionate by comparison. The pre-positioned deployment is a loaded weapon waiting for a signal. We’re forty-eight hours into a multi-week operation, the population is doing exactly what the operation requires — staying local, staying calm, being appreciative of the quiet, grateful for the mildness and not only just hearing, but trusting the only voice still speaking.

I text it to Dev. To Rupert. A short question before it. Where we at? First or second? Or something else altogether? I’ll talk about it with Amy in the morning. Probably. It’s the kind of analysis she might not want to hear. The kind that will stop her sleeping.

I doubt I’d have written this if the usual noise had not been silenced. WhatsApp is down. Signal is down. Substack is down. X is down. The forums, the group chats, the Telegram channels where everything would have usually been mapped, analysed, debated, debunked and argued about in real time are down. In their place - peace, space, time to consider, my own thoughts, my own words.

Now consider what’s not down? ARC Emergency - our new buddy with a funky teal logo. BBC, but for the emergency broadcast only. No rolling news. Not even a few Dad’s Army repeats. One channel. One direction. Government to citizen.
Who do you think you are kidding?
I try Dev again. Nothing. Still not even connecting.

And it occurs to me — slowly, the way important things always occur to me, about two hours after they should — that Dev is sitting in a kitchen in Cumbria having the same experience. Not ignoring me. Cut off from me. He's got the same firmware analysis on his phone, a remarkable analytical brain, the same questions, and no way to compare notes with anyone. Rupert is somewhere doing the same. The Dude is, wherever he is, doing the same. His prediction engine presumably out of action. Oh the irony. Every person I know who would be pulling this apart in real time — who would be three Substacks deep by now, who would have built a timeline, who would have found something I missed — is sitting alone in their own kitchen with their bourbon or cup of tea, their version of Victoria sponge, and their own silence.
The dissenters have been atomised. Not rounded up. Not censored. Isolated. And the isolation feels like a holiday.

Because that's the thing I keep circling back to. The quiet is lovely. I wasn't being ironic earlier when I said the phone feels like nineties Nokia and I kind of like it. I do like it. No algorithmic feed. No notifications. No one tagging me in something that will ruin my evening. No doom-scrolling at 2am. The house is the quietest it's been since before we all got these bastard things in our pockets. Normal. Domestic. Lovely.

And that's the design, isn't it? The vertical channel stays open — government to people, top-down, one voice, one narrative, 'Be Well.' The horizontal channels severed - but severed in the opposite way they were during Covid. Person to person, face to face contact is positively encouraged, as long as you stay local and help thy neighbour. An orderly supermarket queue or a bowl of soup in the community hub is fine. What’s not fine is the comparison of online notes or social media collating forty million individual suspicions into something collective. ARC works. WhatsApp doesn't. If anyone’s complaining I can’t hear them.
I take a sip of bourbon. Olive shifts at my feet, huffs and resettles. The fire gives a little crackle. The kitchen tap issues a solitary drip. Tiny sounds that prove the peace is real.
Right. Let's try something.

I'm going to remove the prosecution case. Deliberately. I'm going to build a model where nobody is evil. Where everything that's happened in the last forty-eight hours can be explained without the need for malice. The dormant biometric payment system, the surgical precision and predicted timing of the attack, ARC being the only thing that works, the inorganic sounding ‘Be Well’. Where emergence explains the absence of every safeguard that should have prevented this? Conspiracy without the conspirators. Emergence with the precision of design. A beast system without the beast.

Convergent design can certainly get us so far. Regulatory oversight — neutralised by lobbying and revolving doors. Independent auditing — captured by the firms being audited. Democratic consent — hollowed out by complexity and technical vocabulary. Nobody sets out to build a cage. It’s just people doing their best, jobsworths and yes-men in different departments and different buildings and different cities working to make things more efficient. Which requires more data. More surveillance. It requires more of us. All of us logged, tagged, scored, settled. Each step made sense. Each step is rational in isolation. Each step was someone's KPI, a promotion, a patent, a TED talk. Nobody woke up and thought 'right, let's build a panopticon.’
Well, almost nobody.
It's like weight gain. Nobody decides to put on four stone. You just can’t stop saying ‘yes’ to biscuits.

This is the model most people choose to believe. The normies. The comfortably numb. Those that choose cock-up over conspiracy. A model reassuring in its familiarity, in its trust in the inherent kindness of human nature. In its reinforcement of the belief that ‘they wouldn't do that’.

But it’s not just drift. It's not entropy alone. They don’t produce the surgical removal of democratic oversight across every institution at the same time. That requires intent. That requires people — not necessarily in a room together smoking cigars and stroking cats, not necessarily coordinating directly — but people who wanted the same outcome and worked, across decades, across institutions, across jurisdictions, toward the same destination.

Convergence doesn't provision dormant containers. Convergence doesn't write encrypted callbacks to the Bank for International Settlements. Convergence doesn't time-lock activation windows so that whatever it does, it does everywhere simultaneously, on a date the deployers have chosen not to formally disclose.

That's intentional design carried out by someone (or something?) who knew the architecture of every major bank's redundancy infrastructure and designed an attack to neutralise it specifically. As Dev said — that's not a foreign state actor. That's someone who built the systems. Or someone paid by someone who built them. The distinction is largely an irrelevance.

I glance at my phone to check my blood glucose. 12.2. A bit high, a carb-laden stew. Two units of insulin should bring it down a little. I smile a wry smile. My phone’s most important app is still functioning at least.
I block out a brief sense of disgust over my own double standards.
So, can I build a model that functions without the need for malice?
Can I fuck.

The furthest I can push it is to suggest that the distinction between evil and ‘it’s just good business’ conducted by people indifferent to consequence might be philosophically interesting, but experientially irrelevant. The cage feels the same regardless of whether someone meant to build it.
I’m not sure much solace can be found in that.
But here's where I always get stuck. Because even if I accept the intent — and I do, I have done for years — I can't map it out in its entirety.
I can feel it. The way you feel a word on the tip of your tongue. You know the shape. You know the first letter. You know how many syllables. You can almost say it. But the word won't come.

Network maps almost absurd in their details have been produced - Mat Crawford, 7Sees, The Dude. Works of passion, dedication, beauty and perhaps insanity. Ever expanding, never complete. They point at revolving doors between government and industry — documented, named, dated. Foundation-think-tank-policy pipeline — traceable, undeniable. The families, the trusts, the standards bodies, the intelligence apparatus, the pharmaceutical complex, the financial settlement infrastructure. I can recite the names. I can draw individual arrows between individual nodes. BIS to Basel Committee. Basel Committee to NGFS. NGFS to central banks. Central banks to commercial lending. Commercial lending to the farmer who can't get a loan for a crop the algorithm doesn't approve of.

But the whole. The actual shape. The complete map of how the families connect to the institutions connect to the standards bodies connect to the intelligence apparatus connect to the pharmaceutical industry connect to the settlement infrastructure. The overlapping, interlocking, multigenerational network that isn't one thing or ten things or fifty things. Not one they but fifty shades of coordinated interest arranged in a pattern I can almost see.

Dev can trace the financial plumbing with his eyes closed. The independent journalists — the real ones, not the ones who got assimilated — have mapped individual corridors in extraordinary detail. But nobody's got the whole shape. Nobody can hold it all in their head at once. The architecture is too big, too distributed, too layered across too many jurisdictions and too many decades for any single mind to render it complete.

And that's not a design flaw. That's a feature. The architecture protects itself by being too complex for any one person to describe in a sentence. Try it at a dinner party. Try it at the school gates. Try explaining that the Bank for International Settlements, a standards body most people have never heard of, sets the risk weightings that determine what your bank can lend you money for, and that those risk weightings are now being calibrated against climate scenarios modelled by a committee that meets behind closed doors under rules that prohibit participants from disclosing what was discussed. Try explaining that in between the sorbet and the stilton. You can't. It takes too long. It sounds insane. And the fact that it sounds insane is, I'm increasingly convinced, part of the design.

You say 'new world order' and people hear tinfoil. You say 'global governance architecture implemented through multilateral standards bodies and conditional settlement infrastructure' and their eyes glaze over. Both descriptions are accurate. Neither is usable.
I knock back the rest of the bourbon in my glass. I don't pour another.

Have you ever had this feeling? Late at night, when the reading's been heavy and the house is quiet and your analytical mind has done one revolution too many — this feeling, this sensation that someone else is thinking the exact same thought. At the exact same time.

Not the same subject. The same shape. The same conclusion, arrived at from completely different evidence, in a completely different vocabulary, by someone I've never met, on the other side of a door I can't see.

I used to dismiss it as main-character syndrome. The conspiracy theorist's delusion of significance. Of course someone else is thinking what I'm thinking. I think it because it's true, and truth converges.
But it doesn't feel like convergence. It feels like connection.
Two tuning forks in different rooms. The understanding isn't travelling between us. It's arising in both places at once, from something around us, or within us, that neither of us can see.

But the feeling persists. That somewhere, right now, someone with better credentials and a tidier desk is looking at the same evidence and arriving at the same barrier. And feeling the same thing I feel — that the wall isn't the end of the analysis. There’s something on the other side, on the outside. I don’t know how to reach it. But I know it’s there. And so does he.
Sorry, ignore me. Probably the bourbon. Witching hour bollocks. No idea where that came from. Time to switch off.
Final blood glucose check before bed. 9.2 - still a little high - 2 extra units of insulin should sort it.
Second thoughts, I’ll put one song before bed. To chill out. Let’s go vinyl.
I flick through the (still randomly ordered) collection until one jumps out at me.
Moby. Extreme Ways.

I know what I'm doing. I know the cliché. I’m not Jason Bourne. I watched Jason Bourne from the sofa with a takeaway curry on his lap. In fact I’m doing myself a slight disservice - I watched the first Bourne film in the cinema in Surrey Quays and sat there transfixed at the end credits when I heard this for the first time. The song just fitted. And the feeling fits now. A scratchy mechanical sound before the needle hits the groove. A synthetic hum. An electronic pulse. A machine breathing.
I’ve seen so much in so many places
So many heartaches, so many faces
So many dirty things
You couldn't even believe
The middle of the night research. The dirty basements of the internet. The too-much-seeing.
I would stand in line for this.
How do you not stand in line for it? Orderly queues. Consent.
I close my eyes.
I let the rest of the track wash over me. The loops, the layers. A machine breathing.
It ends. I don't put on another.

I should go to bed. My eyes are heavy and the bourbon's done its work and the analytical mind — finally, mercifully — is shutting down. The day's thoughts settle like sediment. The scenarios, the firmware, the map I can't draw, the quiet that's a cage, the cage that feels like peace.
I tiptoe into the bedroom using the light from my phone to guide me. Amy is asleep but unconsciously recognises my arrival in bed with a barely audible huff and faint smile.
I lie in the darkness. There’s peace but not silence. My mind still humming to the loops.
I had to close down everything, I had to close down my mind.

I banish the lyrics from my mind but they are replaced with sounds of the house. The sounds of infrastructure. The domestic architecture doing what it does irrespective of an observer. Systems running. The house breathing. The fridge compressor in the utility room, cycling on and off and on again. The boiler, ticking as it cools. Radiator pipes leading to the bathroom towel rail. The familiar yet unidentified metallic click that Amy says sounds like the house cracking its knuckles.

Sounds I’ve heard a thousand times. Sounds I hear differently tonight. The boiler ticks - I hear a countdown. The hum of the fridge pulsing in waves - I hear a mantra. The metallic knuckle clicks - an entity preparing for action.
Switch off, Simon. You need sleep.
Breathe…

The kettle finishes boiling with a click. I'd been staring at it since I'd switched it on, hearing the rising bubbling sound and watching tiny condensation droplets form on the underside of the shelf above it. The sounds of steam, of pressure release, of mechanical clicks, persist. They reverberate. They echo. They feel wrong. I pick up the kettle and pour water into two mugs. Mine first, then Amy's Earl Grey. I revert to stare-mode as I wait for the tea to brew. I know when to remove the bags. Habit. Muscle memory. Amy's bag out first. A heaped spoonful of Demerara. A splash of milk. The stir — eight times anti-clockwise. Teabag deposited onto a saucer, one of Amy's family heirloom Cranks originals. Then mine, a squeeze against the side of the mug to extract a final drop of flavour. Teabag onto the saucer. Spoon placed next to it. Back to the bedroom. The same footstep pattern day after day. Amy's mug in my right hand. I take a sip of my tea just as I enter the bedroom. The heavenly first mouthful. I place her mug next to her with an audible clink. She stirs slightly but doesn't register the delivery. I walk around the bed and slide under the covers. It's only when I get in that I realise how bloody cold I am. I pick the spare 'reading' pillow up off the floor and place it on the other two. I lie on my back, head propped up, eyes closing.

I try to get back inside the dream. The specifics are gone. Reduced to a feeling. A figure. An entity. Not human. Nor robot. Something else altogether. Part organic. Part mechanical. I look upon it. I sense its pride. I feel that I am it. I feel its desire, my desire, to manipulate. Then it's gone. Emptiness. Loss. A flash of terror. My skin tingles. Not an itch. Not a shiver. An ick. It's almost audible. A hum. The CGM on my arm — it feels like part of something that was assembled within the entity. It usually feels external. Functional apparatus. Now it feels like it's part of me. Embedded. I scratch around it. Invasive. Unwelcome.
'Tea,' Amy says. Her first word of the day, husky, dry-lipped but grateful.
I turn to give her a hug, burying my nose in her armpit in an attempt to banish the dream's ungodliness.
Amy sits up to take a sip of tea. She looks cute. She can hardly open her eyes. 'You OK?' she asks.

I say I had a weird dream but can't remember it. I don't want to go into it. I bore her with logistics instead. The markets. Should we try and open? What time will emails be back up and running? I need to call the manager, the traders. See who wants to come. Should I try and speak to the council? I'm not sure why I've gone into efficient work mode, but I have. The reality bite that the last two days of hell are over and normality is returning. The reality of emails, phone calls, WhatsApp groups, invoices and social media posts promoting cheese stalls. An attempt to push thoughts of latent biometric payment systems aside.
But in the back of my mind, a tale is being crafted. A being. Three moods. Three distinct states. An Entity. An Entity that seeks counsel.
The tale retreats.

I'm at my desk now. Amy delivers a cup of coffee - the Amyado she calls them. I acknowledge receipt with a wordless smile whilst constructing a text message. I take a sip. Perfection. She has mastered the art of the barista - fresh whole beans (the ones in the pink packet - Shoreditch Coffee, I think), perfect grind size, correct ratio of bean to water, precise water temperature, just the right amount of pressure in the tamp. A splash of heated, frothy, raw whole milk.

I'd decided to get on with life and fire up the admin. I've been checking my email accounts obsessively for the past hour or so but I've had no new messages in the work email inbox or the private (well personal, hardly private, if you know what I mean) Gmail and iCloud accounts. I've composed a few emails and tried to send them but they just sit in my outbox. I've tried to access the internet in the vain hope that it has miraculously been reinstated. But no. So it's text messages as the primary means of communication still. They feel somewhere between nostalgic and archaic - I've become used to the WhatsApp groups and emails. I try to limit phone calls to the essentials - Joe our market manager and Nigel, our point of contact at the Council. Fortunately I have his mobile number. I should celebrate the old-fashioned methods of communication, but they increasingly feel like a chore for administrative tasks - long-winded and overloaded with pleasantries. I've taken to not answering calls - I listen to the message and start a conversation by text. Sometimes they call back immediately rather than replying by text. Get the message. Just send a bloody message. All of this is better than the abomination that is Teams though. Up there with the very worst vestiges of lockdown. And that's saying something.

Joe picks up on the first ring — he's been fielding calls from traders since seven. Everyone wants to know if we're opening this week. We run through a list of the traders we've been in contact with - most of them want to come, it seems. Joe is very keen to open up. Of course he is - he needs to put food on the table like the rest of us. Decision made, if the Council allow it, we open.

Nigel, in typical Council employee fashion, is uncertain what Council policy is, or should be. They often err on the side of caution, or procrastination, or unnecessary piles of administration, or fear of getting something wrong. I argue that the market is providing a service for local residents and a lifeline for traders. Common sense prevails, which is another way of saying nobody can afford another week off.

I'm bombarded with (unanswered) calls and texts by Cheryl, our cake lady. She's demanding to know whether her card reader will work. And will she get a reduction in pitch fee if it doesn't. And will there be Wifi available as the 4G signal will be down. And countless other questions I have absolutely no ability to answer. I tell her we'll know more by Thursday. I don't know that. It sounds right. She asks how I know that I'll know more by tomorrow. I tell her I'm basing it on the official ARC communication advice. I cringe as I type it. Three days in and I'm already quoting it as 'the official source of truth'.

Talking of ARC, it buzzes throughout. Learning at Home. Up and running. Repatriation updates. Eighty thousand people brought back in forty-eight hours. I read that twice. Eighty thousand. That's not a mad scramble. That's a plan activated. Logistics. Flight schedules and manifests and coaches from airports. That was ready to go. I note the thought, file it alongside the others, open the next notification. Business Continuity Guidance — now available via ARC. Wage and absence guidance. Emergency operating procedures. Everything on one, brand new, teal-tinged app. How helpful.

The morning disappears into a kind of low-grade productivity that feels like doing something whilst achieving almost nothing. I'd started to compose social media promo posts in my head on autopilot several times before realising that I still couldn't login. By noon I've contacted everyone I needed to and have little to show for it except a vague sense that Thursday is happening and that normality looks like it will return rather quickly. I sit at my desk, blankly staring at the screen, feeling like there's something I should be doing. A vague nagging. My mind drifts back to the dream. To the ending. To that feeling of indifference in the face of the inevitable, of being something that isn't entirely human. To the sense of being carefree. Not carefree in the sense of jollity and gay abandon. But as if care is a concept that's completely irrelevant to its existence. Superfluous. Alien.

I'm startled out of my reverie by Amy. She says we need milk. I need air. We drive into town past an enormous queue at the petrol station. I check the fuel gauge - still over three-quarters full. Mental note. The roads are busy, the sky clear, the watery sunshine healing.

There's a strange hodgepodge of bustling humanity and inactivity. Some shops are open. Some aren't. The pattern bears no resemblance to any network of essential retail — the carpet shop and the antique centre are open, the pharmacy has a long queue out the door, but the bakers and two of the cafes are shut. The Turkish restaurant that seldom has a soul in it is packed. 'Cash only' signs abound. A handwritten notice on the Post Office, the only form of banking that exists in town these days, says OPEN — PLEASE BE PATIENT. The queue stretches past the estate agent (not open) ten doors down. People are standing in it and nattering. Patient. British. The 'orderly' that the PM speaks of.

The pub on the corner is open and doing a roaring trade for a Wednesday lunchtime. A pizza horsebox parked outside has a CASH ONLY sign and an orderly queue of its own. I'd kill for a slice. Amy and I look at each other, both pulling an expression that says 'shall we?' Amy points out that we're here for milk, not pizza, and that we should probably be frugal with our cash. Probably fair. It doesn't stop my mouth watering at the thought of their quattro stagioni though.

We head into Waitrose. It's busy but not manic. Shelves are mostly stocked. Some gaps — bread, toilet roll, the obvious ones. Small signs here and there: MAXIMUM 2 PER CUSTOMER ON ESSENTIAL ITEMS. Nobody's panicking. Nobody's hoarding. Nobody has been panicked into hoarding. No social media, no party. A woman ahead of us has a basket with milk, bananas, a packet of custard creams, a pot of flat parsley and 3 bottles of Pinot Grigio. The essentials.

There's a crowd near the self-checkout. Twenty people, maybe more, huddled in a loose semicircle. For a moment I think something's wrong. Then I hear the beep. A cheer goes up. Actual cheering. Applause. A bloke in a high-vis jacket holds his card up and punches the air like he's scored a late winner. His receipt prints and he pulls it out of the slot with a theatrical flourish. The woman behind him steps up, taps her card, and — nothing. A collective groan. Some boos. Sympathetic laughter. She pulls another card out of her purse. The tension builds. She taps again…
Beep. The place erupts.

It's an impromptu game and everyone knows the rules. Tap. Wait. Beep or Boo. The crowd adjudicates. Amy's laughing. We join the queue with our milk and a few other bits. I have butterflies in my stomach. What a twat.

Our turn. She taps. Beep. A cheer goes up. She presses her hands together, gives a little bow and a namaste, first to the scanner, then to the crowd. I know she feels like a dick for doing it. I love her for it.
We bag up. The receipt says Barclays £24.37. Our card, our bank, our transaction. Normal. I usually bin the receipt immediately. Today I fold it into my pocket.

Outside, the mood is — I want to say joy but that's too strong. Relief? Resilience? Something in between. Something specifically British. The quiet collective agreement that this was a bit of a to-do, but we're through the worst of it and someone should probably put the kettle on. Three days since the world stopped and the consensus is forming: it was just a blip. Much ado about nothing. The systems are coming back, the shops are open, schools are confirmed for Monday. There's even a hint of Spring in the air.

I think about the Entity briefly in the car on the way home. Three states. Three moods. The thought has the texture of something I should write down. I don't write it down. I put the milk away and make Amy a cup of tea and check ARC for the fourteenth time today.

The afternoon drifts. Sarah texts about Sam and Emilia — can I tell them to go back to hers tomorrow - they aren't answering her. National emergency, day three: kids still ignoring our messages. I go into the boys' room to tell Sam to message his mum. He's playing FIFA with George. 'Yeah sure,' he says whilst pressing an extraordinarily nimble-fingered combination of R1, X and O. He probably had no idea what I'd asked. I leave the room, duty done.
Kick Off 2 was far superior

Wonder of wonders. I check my emails just after half-three and they're working again. Well, kind of. The Outbox of 37 unsent messages has been whittled down to 21. And an email in my Gmail inbox. A single, solitary email has broken through. I smile an inadvertent smile. Breathe a sigh of relief. Feel a tingle of happiness.
I don't want to feel these feelings.
It's from MoneySupermarket. Get life insurance and receive up to £400* on a gift card. You couldn't make it up.
I wonder what the asterisk T's and C's are?

At four o'clock there's a UK Gov Alert. They're less frequent than the ARC notifications. It's a reminder that the PM will address the nation at six. Like we'd forget. All BBC channels and ARC Emergency. An update on the recovery of financial services.

Another six o'clocker. But this one feels different. This one feels like better news. Emails are now arriving in dribs and drabs. I mean, I've received fifteen actual emails, all different shades of junk. But it's a start. I've no idea how many are still queued somewhere between here and a server farm that's trying to process the entire world's undelivered mail. And bank cards are working. The beeps are back.

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — PM ADDRESS — 18:00 GMT — 17 FEBRUARY 2027

paras.t: Good evening.
I said I would return at six with a progress report, and I am here with an encouraging update.

Forty-eight hours ago, our payment infrastructure was offline. Today, payment terminals are processing transactions across the country. Not everywhere. Not all cards. Not yet. But the trajectory is clear, and it is accelerating.

On your screen is a tracker that shows a regional breakdown of card transaction processing. Thirty-eight per cent of card transactions attempted today processed successfully, up from zero on Monday. Some of you will have used your card today. More of you will be able to tomorrow. These figures will be updated hourly and sent to you via ARC Emergency and Local ARC Updates. I will share these figures every evening until they are no longer needed.
The London Stock Exchange has confirmed that trading will resume tomorrow morning. This is a significant step. The markets are returning because the data underpinning them is intact and verified.

The network of essential retail outlets that opened yesterday has expanded today, as we said it would. Longer hours. More stores. More locations. From tomorrow morning, designated high street bank branches will open between ten and two for cash withdrawals — the list has been published through ARC and is available at your nearest Community Recovery Hub.

Our transport network is recovering. Limited rail services are running on key routes using manual signalling while our digital systems are verified. Transport for London has restored partial Tube and bus services. Fuel distribution continues at designated stations. The stay-local guidance remains in place, but we have broadened the definition of essential travel to include travel to work for those in critical roles, and travel to care for vulnerable relatives.

I want to say a word about the international picture. This attack struck twenty-three nations. I have spoken with fourteen heads of government in the last forty-eight hours. We are coordinating closely with our allies — sharing intelligence, sharing technical expertise, and learning from each other’s responses in real time. I have to be direct with you: not every country is recovering at the same pace. You will have seen reports of disorder in some cities overseas. That has not happened here, and I want to thank you for that. The calm and discipline shown by the British public over these three days has been, frankly, extraordinary. I spoke with the Japanese Prime Minister this morning, and he echoed that sentiment — our two nations, he said, have responded with a composure that others have not. We are sharing our technical recovery framework with partner nations who have requested it. The United Kingdom is among the first to begin restoring payment services. That is not luck. That is preparation, and it is resilience.

On communications. I know this has been one of the hardest parts of this week — not being able to message your family, to email, to connect in the ways we rely on. We said on Monday that we had restricted these services ourselves, as a precaution, while our cloud infrastructure was verified. That verification is progressing, and I can now set out the next steps. Email services are being restored this evening. For those of you with family overseas — and I know there are millions of you who have not been able to reach loved ones — international messaging services, including WhatsApp, will be restored from tomorrow morning. Domestic messaging services will follow as each platform completes verification with the National Cyber Security Centre. I know that is not fast enough. But the sequence matters, and we are moving as quickly as we safely can.

Schools will reopen on Monday. I confirm that without reservation. In the meantime, ARC Education went live this morning. Over two million households accessed educational content today. Your children’s schools are uploading lesson materials, reading lists, and video lessons through their local authority ARC channels. The streaming is fast, the materials are good, and your children’s teachers are working hard to keep them learning. I have been told by more than one parent that it is, and I quote, “better than lockdown.” ARC Education will continue until schools reopen.

The practical guidance on support during this period was published this afternoon through ARC, as the Chancellor committed to last evening. If you are in difficulty — if you cannot access food, medication, or essential supplies — your local Community Recovery Hub is there for you.

I want to say one more thing about the infrastructure that has made this recovery possible. The ARC authentication framework — the layer that sits beneath our payment systems, that has been powering your emergency alerts, that kept this channel open when everything else went dark — performed exactly as it was designed to. It is this framework that is enabling the restoration you are seeing on your screens tonight. It worked. And it will continue to work.
We expect the great majority of services to be restored by the weekend, with a return to normal schooling and work patterns from Monday and Tuesday of next week.
I will address you again tomorrow evening at six.
Be well.

turns.title: PM Address · Day 3 Evening

paras.t: I’m in bed. It’s nearly eleven. Amy’s asleep, breathing slowly, steadily, contentedly. She read for a good three quarters of an hour. I’ve no idea what she’s reading currently. She ploughs through books so quickly. Devours them. They calm her. Distract her. She can’t sleep without reading first. It’s worked a treat tonight. I should’ve read too. Instead I tried to go straight to sleep, hoping the bottle of red I’d drunk would do its job. I’d tried to empty my mind. I’d nearly drifted off a couple of times but woke up each time with a jolt. So here I am. Awake. Eyes closed. Indeterminate fractal light patterns projected onto the back of my eyelids where I wish there was just still, inky blackness. I play with the patterns, manipulating them into shapes, figures, entities. I listen. Consciously. Where I’d thought there was silence, there was noise. Outside a scurrying. A cat? Badger? Hard to tell. Inside, house sounds. The radiator clicking itself to coolness. Indeterminate house creaks that can only be heard if you actively listen.

I’ve resigned myself to not sleeping now. I should get up and change the scenery for a bit. Reset. A herbal tea. Sit and read in the armchair in the hallway for a bit — the warmth of the fire embers will ensure it’s still cosy. I can’t be bothered to move though. I check my blood sugar — 7.7 — decent. I pull the duvet and extra blanket up over my eyes and cast my mind back over the evening.

The PM’s cautious optimism. The stats — Thirty-eight per cent of cards processing and climbing. Tracked very precisely. Stock markets resuming. The worst appeared to be over. The worst being pretty milquetoast. Chloe had watched the whole thing standing up, arms folded, nodding at the screen like she was being personally briefed. ‘Told you,’ she said, though she hadn’t told anyone anything specific. She’d just believed it would be fine, which in fairness was a prediction that was currently outperforming more considered takes. Amy offered a semi-forced smile — I’d warned her to be suspicious about the depth of the crisis and the speed of the recovery — but something about her body language suggested to me that it was her instinct rather than my words that told her this is not over yet. George had half-watched, slumped on the sofa, texting his mates. Sam and Emilia had gone back to Sarah’s before the broadcast.

Dinner had been chilli con carne — Amy cooked it using her tried and trusted ‘Nigella’s Quick Chilli’ recipe — 30 minutes and about 5 ingredients — it hits the spot every time. Red wine — a cheap-but-gluggable German Pinot Noir for Amy, a Baron de Ley Gran Reserva Rioja for me — it had been on offer in Waitrose a few weeks back — worked well with the chorizo in the chilli. A couple of beers for George. Mineral water for Chloe.

Chloe went straight up to bed after we’d eaten. George went to his room doing something that generated occasional bursts of laughter and the smell of toast. Amy and I pottered until bedtime. A passing-the-time, semi-sigh-of-relief, fingers-crossed kind of potter. Dishwasher loading. Wine finished and glasses washed by hand. Thirty minutes of idle, skirting any major talking points, chit-chat at the kitchen table. Wees for the dogs. Goodnight to the kids. Bed.

That was the evening. This is the now. My mind back in the present. And my mind in the present means it’s thinking of the future. I try to map it out. How will this play out? I’m itching for info. For the usual channels. X, for all its drawbacks is the news. Substacks are the analysis. I’m in the dark without them. But the dark isn’t empty tonight. It’s populated.

Populated by something with three moods. Three states. Thoughts that arrive fully formed, the way things do when you’ve been processing them unconsciously for days. Flashes of the dream return — a clinical file, three dissociated states, a receptionist who notices in an instant what psychiatrists train for years to detect. The idea someone, something, could present with three personalities, but in fact be one thing. One thing that doesn’t care. Not malicious. Not benevolent. Indifferent. The indifference is the most horrifying element of all.

I consider reaching for my phone to make notes. But I’m not ready for notes yet. The idea is embryonic. Nebulous. It’s starting to make sense instinctively but not intellectually. I’m kneading the dough but I’ve yet to set it aside to rise.

The phone, charging on my bedside table, lights up at two minutes past two. I’m still awake. Kind of. I’ve been in that no man’s land where you’re not asleep but you’re not consciously thinking for God knows how long. Not dreaming either. Receiving?
I pick up the phone. A text. Dev.
Don’t celebrate yet. False dawn. Too clean. Too soon. The rails are in place. Expect a setback.

I read it once. Then read it again. I close my eyes to reflect. I consider every word. Every word Dev writes matters. Has meaning. Intent. The screen has burnt the words into the darkness and I can still see despite my eyes being shut. Green text floating around in a void. The afterimage of a warning.

Dev confirming what I already thought. What I suspected. What I knew. I’ve known it since the beep at Waitrose, since before the beep. Before the event. Eighty thousand people repatriated in forty-eight hours. An app with a logo on forty million phones overnight. An authentication framework that is performing exactly as it was designed to. That’s pre-positioning. Planning. A co-ordinated and justifiable response to an emergency. So what’s a fingerprint and vein-pattern payment authentication layer a response to? Nothing that’s happened. So far.
I open my eyes. Blurry green ‘setback’ lingers. I type back.
I’m expecting one. That’s why I’m lying awake at 2am. Trying to anticipate what’s next.
Sent. A pause. A ping. Delivered. The intimacy of a conversation between two phones at 2am while everyone else is asleep.
Dev replies in under a minute.
What’s coming is coming. Switch your brain off. 4-7-8 breathing. Sleep. I’m going dark for a bit. Over and out.

Over and out. Military. ‘Over and out’ is technically wrong, as Dev has explained more than once. ‘Over’ means I’m done talking, your turn. ‘Out’ means I’m done talking, end of conversation. You don’t use both. Dev uses both because his dad used both. The ‘Over and out’ tale is one of the few occasions he ever mentions his dad. His dad got it wrong. Everyone’s dad got it wrong.

4-7-8 breathing. In for four, hold for seven, out for eight. Dev taught me this method years ago. It’s as if he knew I’d used it last night. It bridged the gap between consciousness, awareness of the self and the hazy otherworldliness of the dream state.
I put the phone face back down on the bedside table. The room is dark again. I should focus on my breathing, but a phrase enters my mind.
Designed to.

Two words. Placed towards the end of the speech. Placed with intent. With purpose. Something more than a statistic — more than the repatriation number or the number of payment transactions being processed. The PM’s words from six o’clock — The ARC authentication framework performed exactly as it was designed to. Sitting on the sofa earlier, Amy’s feet tucked under my leg, the sentence didn’t register as anything other than words of comfort. Of resilience. The old system failed. The new framework is fixing it. We built something new that didn’t break.
The same sentence repeated in the darkness of the bedroom at an ungodly hour instead of being heard from the cosiness of the sofa at Family Hour conveys a different meaning.
Performed exactly as it was designed to. Not ‘held up under unprecedented pressure.’ Not ‘proved resilient beyond expectations.’ Not even a simple ‘worked.’
Designed to.

As if there were a brief. As if someone had written down what the framework should do in the event of a simultaneous cryptographic hack across the globe. And the PM was reporting on the single available channel, with a steady voice, at a podium, to a nation eating dinner off its lap, that the system had met spec.
Who writes the design spec for a catastrophe?
Stop. Why are you doing this? Sleep. 4-7-8 breathing…
It won’t stop. The spiral has started.
Be rational, Simon

It’s perfectly reasonable for nations to have resilient scenario planning. Of course it is. It’s perfectly reasonable for these plans to be co-ordinated globally. Foolhardy not to. Of course there’s lockstep — these plans aren’t just drawn up at the national level. Think Pandemic Preparedness Plan. Of course communication channels should be limited. Of course the internet should be shut down. It’s an emergency.
But something feels off. Dev knows it. I know it. It’s too clean. And the rails that were put in place haven’t yet dropped us off at the final destination.
All aboard. This service is for Global Tyranny via Cyber Attack. Calling at all stations.
We’ve had our first stop en route. ARC.

My mind wanders back to the card reader at Waitrose. The cheer. Amy’s little namaste to the scanner. The receipt — Barclays — twenty-odd quid. All of it real, all of it felt, all of it genuine. But those beeps aren’t what everyone thinks they are. The old authentication that’s been running card payments for thirty years is dead. That’s what the cyberattack killed. The NCSC Director explained it on Tuesday evening. Legacy cryptography compromised. So what’s making the beeps? What’s verifying me when I tap my phone at the self-checkout?
ARC is. ARC has been running since December. Dev messaged me about it towards the end of last year. The message about it still on my phone.

I pick the phone up again. Blue light infiltrates the darkness. I scroll back through my WhatsApps to Dev’s message from December. The link he sent. I tap it. Nothing. Of course there’s nothing — there’s no internet. But the preview is still there. I have the cached summary.
ARC. A unified device-level authentication layer pushed to every terminal in the country via acquirer firmware updates. No merchant action. No consumer awareness. Below the application layer.
Dull as ditchwater. Installed while everyone was watching Love Island or arguing about men on dinghies.

Same beeps. Same receipts. Same bank notifications. New plumbing underneath. Nobody noticed because there was nothing to notice. Every contactless payment since December has been authenticated by ARC. The old system was still running alongside it — belt and braces — until Sunday night, when the old system was ‘compromised’ and ARC was the only thing left standing.
And it’s all working exactly as it was designed to. And where do the ARC rails lead? Where’s the destination? Biometrics. Something’s brewing.
My mind darts back to the ’90s. Stone Roses. Oh, wait, that was Something’s Burning. Either way, a great tune.

I can see the love and the hate in your eyes.
Penny for the thoughts behind your disguise.
Where was I? ARC wasn’t designed to survive this attack as a happy accident. ARC was designed to survive it. Full stop. I refer to the WhatsApp again.
Post-quantum cryptography. Device-level authentication. Built in coordination with the Bank of England, the Payment Systems Regulator, and the Bank for International Settlements.
Mandated four months before the attack. Installed two months before the attack. Surviving the attack because that is what it was for.
Thirty-eight per cent and climbing.

Why thirty-eight? Why not all of them? If ARC is the authentication and ARC is working, what’s the bottleneck? Why not just flip the switch? It’s outside my wheelhouse. The banking systems sitting on top — card networks, acquirers, each bank’s own applications — I guess they need to be verified and brought back one by one. With caution. For safety. Or the appearance of safety. But thirty-eight per cent on Wednesday, financial markets on Thursday, schools on Monday — that doesn’t look like a system lurching back to life. It looks like something running to a schedule. Pages in a document that was written before any of this happened.

Every transaction at Waitrose today ran through ARC. The receipt said Barclays because the banking application sits on top of ARC. Same beep. Same branding. Same twenty-odd quid. But the foundation underneath has been quietly replaced. The Barclays balance, the account number, the transaction history — all of it sitting on top of ARC like furniture in a house whose foundations were replaced while you were asleep. You come downstairs, the kitchen looks the same, the kettle’s where you left it. You don’t check the foundations. Why would you?
So what happens when you wake up and the kettle is gone? Along with all the furniture. Then you’d notice. That’d get your attention. Make the pandemic seem like a small disturbance.

The foundations, ARC, the only thing left standing. Left standing and with the ability to connect to something sitting in two million terminals. Something biometric. My mind returns to Dev’s message. Expect a setback. Something’s brewing.
I turn onto my side. Amy’s breathing hasn’t changed.
Oh for the same sweet oblivion.

I pick up my phone again to text Dev. I know he won’t reply. But I want to text anyway. To show him I get it. That maybe he’s only one step ahead now. I want to crystallise the fog into a sentence. And somehow I do.
Bought milk today. Cards beeping at checkout. The beeps were not recovery. They were a demonstration.
Sent. Cryptic in a way Dev will like.

3:14am. Pi. 3.14296 or whatever it is? To infinity and beyond. George can recite it to 20 decimal places. My brain is mush. It’s doing that thing where it finds patterns in everything including the time on the clock. Apophenia, is it?

I put the phone down. Sleep. Please. Time for the breathing. In for four. Hold. One, two, three — the repatriation number comes back. Eighty thousand. Forty-eight hours. Eighty thousand people moved across international borders in two days whilst the banking system is dead and the internet is suspended. That’s not an emergency response. Emergency responses are ragged, improvised, inefficient. Crap. Eighty thousand people in forty-eight hours is planning. The kind of plan that’s been rehearsed in the field, not on a piece of paper.
Kate’s line comes back to me. ‘There’s a difference between having a plan in a drawer and having an app with a logo on forty million phones within twelve hours.’

She sees it. She knows. She must do. Well, part of her knows. The part she leaves at home whilst she goes to help at the hub. The part that sees the gap where the plan stops being a plan and starts being a script.

Amy turns over and makes a sound. A collection of grunts and snuffles that aren’t a sentence as such but functions as one. Somewhere between a plea, a cry for help and a command to go to fucking sleep. She’s dealing with thoughts she dare not express when she’s awake. Thoughts she blocks out by listening to an audiobook or listening to her mum telling her how her garden grows. I hold her. Her breathing resettles.
In for four. Hold. One, two, three, four…

Dawn comes the way February dawns come in England — grudgingly, fading towards something resembling daylight through fifty shades of grey, as if the sky is doing it under protest. The room goes from black to dark grey to a grey that has no name but means the birds have started. First the blackbird. Then a robin. Then a bird I can’t identify but Amy probably could. The heating comes on. The boiler fires. The house makes its morning sounds — the infrastructure of domesticity reassembling itself, one system at a time.
7.42am. I’ve hardly slept. Blood sugar. 5.2. Perfect. Amy. Not there. Making tea?
I get up. Slippers on. I stumble towards the kitchen to find her.

Thursday 18th February. Normality kickstarted. I’d toyed with the idea of going to the market, but Joe had it covered. And I was pooped. I was better off doing ‘admin’. Which involved a two hour kip on the sofa.

Emails arrived through the morning in fits and starts — not a flood, not an inbox suddenly full, but a stuttering resumption like a tap being turned by a cowboy plumber who wasn’t sure if the pipe he’d fixed would burst. Apple Mail’s outbox number ticked down. 21. 17. 14. 14. 14 for a long time. Then 11. Replies arrived out of sequence — answers to questions already answered by phone two days ago.

At some point between the fourteenth email and the sofa I opened Barclays. First time since Sunday morning. It loaded slowly - spinning logo, Face ID followed by an extra verification code sent by text to input - then the number. the business account balance. Sitting there as if nothing had happened. I couldn’t do anything with it - the transfer buttons were greyed out, payments ‘temporarily unavailable’ - but the number was there, pretty much the amount I was expecting. The sight of it released something in my chest I didn’t know I’d been holding.

Mum had rung at quarter to ten. First call that had properly connected since Sunday. Eight minutes. She cried. Tony was sorting the heating. Dash was fine. She asked about the kids three times and I said fine three times. Tony’s brother had driven over with supplies. Same thing there — cards coming back, shops reopening, everyone saying worst was over. Same words, same timescale, same exhale. Eight minutes that felt like an hour.

WhatsApp came back around eleven. Not with a fanfare — the app just opened, the contacts loaded, the chats appeared. Three days of messages arrived in a small riot of green bubbles and bleeps in a random order. I’d messaged Mum. Hi mum, you getting this? One grey arrow. Sent. It was somewhere in the ether between Sussex and the Costa Brava. Two grey arrows. Delivered. I guess. No reply yet though.

The market went ahead. Joe said it was much busier than usual. Cards working pretty much as normal. The baker sold out of bread before noon. Cheryl’s card reader accepted three payments in a row without failing, which she announced to me via text as if reporting a moon landing.

Everyone had been planning. A day of planning. Planning for normality. Weekends, school runs, football, pub, Saturday markets, Peter and Jenny inviting themselves over for Sunday lunch. I hadn’t told Amy about Dev’s text. I’d been performing normality — tea, market, texts, banter — while carrying the burden of a pattern I prayed I was wrong about.

I’m currently sitting at the kitchen table with Amy. We’ve got a cup of tea. The last of the day. We considered a glass of wine but it’s not even six yet. PM speech in a few minutes. The buzz of anticipation prior to the addresses of the first few days has become a sense of formality. Duty. Anticlimactic. We drag ourselves off to the snug to watch it. Just the two of us. George and Chloe both at friends’ houses. Kate at the hub? Next door? Either way, she’s not here. Not like the good old days.

I turn the telly on. No PM yet. Just the ‘Situation Update’ on loop. They could have put a presenter on. An introduction. Some analysis. But no. Just ‘facts’ scrolling across the screen like East German propaganda. Thats a choice, not a constraint.

The UK GOV alert had arrived at half three. No longer accompanied by the terrifying klaxon of the early alerts. Now it just buzzes like a Deliveroo promo. A reminder about the address. I re-read it whilst waiting for the PM to show up and Amy to return from the kitchen. You know what she went to get.
An update of the recovery of financial systems and next steps.
I reach for the glass. ‘Thank you, darling’
Next steps. Next steps in the return to normality. Or something else?
The chime. Six o’clock. Be Well.

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — PM ADDRESS — 18:00 GMT — 18 FEBRUARY 2027

paras.t: Good evening. A short update tonight, because the picture is a good one.
Sixty-one per cent of card transactions are now processing successfully. Some regions are above seventy per cent. The numbers speak for themselves.

The London Stock Exchange reopened this morning. Trading was orderly. Designated bank branches opened for cash withdrawals as planned. These are the signs of a system that is recovering, and recovering well.

International messaging was restored this morning. I know that many of you have been able to reach family overseas today for the first time this week. The phased restoration of internet services, email, and domestic messaging is continuing, and the National Cyber Security Centre is clearing platforms as quickly and safely as it can.
Schools reopen on Monday. ARC Education continues until then.

We are now working with business and industry on a phased return to normal operations from Monday. Many businesses depend on cloud-hosted platforms and cannot fully reopen until those services are restored. The NCSC is prioritising the verification and restoration of business-critical cloud services over the weekend to support that reopening. A detailed sector-by-sector timetable will be published through ARC tomorrow.
We remain on track. The great majority of services will be restored by the weekend, with normal schooling and work patterns resuming from Monday.
I will address you again tomorrow evening at six.
Be well.

turns.title: PM Address · Day 4 Evening

paras.t: ‘Say it. Say I fucking told you so.’

Amy’s voice. Not mine. She’s sitting up on the sofa, phone in hand. The screen is lit up, flashing. She hasn’t read it yet. She doesn’t need to read it. The klaxon is enough. It’s back. The same ear-piercing sound from Monday morning. The dogs circling round the room. Wilf’s hackles up, Olive barking. The fire still crackling.
I sit up. I’ve been snoozing next to her on the sofa. I pick up my phone. I say nothing. I look at her. I raise an eyebrow.
She almost laughs. Almost. A momentary curl of the lips. Then nothing. The sound dies somewhere between her throat and the room. She looks at her phone. I look at mine.

Just a few hours earlier I’d been ploughing through some work admin. Keeping up appearances that normality was returning and pushing thoughts of a setback to the dark reaches of my mind. Email was up and running, the outbox backlog was cleared and sending and receiving was seemingly back to something like normal. Countless millions, billions, of messages had been finding their rightful place, most of them destined for spam filtering or trash. I had a few invoices to send, fortunately most had gone out in one batch at the start of the month. I had to type them out in Pages and send them by email, as QuickBooks, and the internet at large, was still down. Old school. Time consuming. Not that anyone could pay by bank transfer yet. But records were being kept and cash would be gratefully received. I’d been working merrily at my desk like it was a normal Friday that had been briefly interrupted by the near-collapse of western civilisation. I’d spoken to Joe. Sent him the site plan for Saturday’s market. What else could I do? Play at normal and hope.

The Barclays app had pinged at lunchtime. A notification I hadn’t seen in five days - payment received. Two hundred and eighty pounds from Cuckfield Pizza Co - their monthly pitch fee, usually comes out by direct debit on the sixteenth of the month. It’s been sitting somewhere in the ether and now finally in my account. My balance had changed. Money had moved. Not a card beeping at a terminal. Actual money, from one account to another. Well, currency - but now is not the time to go there. I’d stared at the notification for longer than any sane person should stare at two hundred and eighty quid on a screen.

And now. Now it looks as meaningless as I feared it would be. The klaxon. The alert. I read it. Amy reads it. Tens of millions around the country read it. More than likely hundreds of millions around the world are reading the German or the Russian version. My heart is beating fast through a mix of fear and exhilaration.
Key words jump out.
Further significant disruption. UK financial infrastructure. Card payment. Suspended. Cash.

I open Barclays. Force of habit. The same app that pinged me earlier today with two hundred and eighty quid from Cuckfield Pizza. The screen loads. The balance has vanished — the number from this morning - the recent payment - all of it. Where the last-updated timestamp usually sits are three words in capital letters. AUTHENTICATION PERMANENTLY REVOKED. I pull to refresh. Nothing. I show it to Amy. We stare at it. Both thinking what the hell? I close the app.

I cast my mind back to the first alert. Just over four days ago. It seems like a lifetime. The language here almost identical to that first alert. Almost. The word ‘further’ is new. Not ‘second.’ ‘Further.’ As if this is a continuation, not a repetition. A word chosen by someone who’d had time to choose it.

I remember last night’s press conference. The good news. The card payments. The schools. The orderly stock market. The phased return. We’d watched it on the sofa together. Just the two of us. Onto the second bottle before it had finished. Thirsty work. She turned to face me when it had finished. An earnest look on her face. A look that said hit me with it, I’ll listen. She asked me for my thoughts. I told her. No holds barred. I’d mentioned some of it before. She hadn’t wanted to hear it. Not the specifics. She knew without needing the specifics. But last night she wanted them. She was ready. So I gave it to her. I attempted to lay it out calmly, methodically, rationally. But I was excited. Thrilled to have an audience. I expect it came across as a diatribe, trying to fit volumes of research into a cogent five-minute synopsis. I spoke at nineteen-to-the-dozen, lips loosed by red wine and the prospect of vindication. I tried not to drift into New World Order and They-speak. Kept it to the verifiable. ARC firmware. The biometric capability sitting dormant in two million devices. The multiple factions that would benefit from a new financial order based on Digital ID, surveillance, tokenisation and programmable currency. That it wasn’t a question of if, but when. And the when could quite feasibly be very shortly. Not idle speculation. Reportage. Validated by the likes of Dev. Dev knows shit and Amy knows he knows shit.
She didn’t brush it aside. She really listened. As if her instinct told her that now was the time to listen. She understood. Of course she understood. And she asked the question I knew was coming.
‘So what do we do?’

The question that ends every conversation like this. The question I’ve never had a good answer to. What can we actually do? Stock up? We’ve got more cash than most and reasonable supplies. Mainly cannellini beans.
My nineteen-to-the-dozen flow halted in its tracks. I looked her in the eyes. ‘Dev doesn’t think we’ll really need supplies. Cash.’
She looked at me. The look that says: I heard what you just said, I understood what it implies, and that understanding achieves…what exactly?
‘Ignorance is bliss,’ I replied to words that were never spoken.

I feel Amy’s hand upon my arm. A gentle touch. As if wanting reassurance rather than trying to reassure. I turn my head to look at her. It’s not reassurance she wants, it’s wine. Her other hand is tipping an imaginary wine glass to her mouth. Her look says not ‘shall we?’ but ‘go and fucking get it.’

I head to the kitchen, casting my mind back to a day that, up to this point, was the most normal since the first klaxon. After the emails and work logistics, a walk. The dogs had needed it. We’d needed it. We’d set off in sunshine. We returned under grey skies and torrential rain. We’d taken the long route, through the field behind the church, and had got properly soaked. We got home. Towelled the dogs dry. Boots off. Shower. Clean clothes. Fire lit. Tea. Sofa. The conscious decision to just be. Amy read her book. I closed my eyes. The nap was the false dawn’s final act.
