I pull a bottle of red from the rack. It’s a Pommard. Set aside for an occasion. Fuck it. This wasn’t the occasion I had in mind but, whatever. Two glasses. I head back to Amy. Part of me is terrified. Part of me is vindicated. Part of me is emboldened. Part of me is something I don’t have a word for — the feeling of having been right about the thing you most wanted to be wrong about. Fear and validation in the same breath. They shouldn’t coexist. They do.

The phones start chirping. George first, quickest on the draw, as always. I text Dev, Rupert. The same two words. Who knew? More texts, a few calls. Not many connect. Network jammed. No WhatsApp again - it never got past the ‘international message’ phase - I managed to send precisely one message since it was reinstated.

We sit. We wait. We pick at a board of cheese and wild boar salami. We drink wine. The Pommard is exceptional. Domaine Nicolas Rossignol. 2019. Deep, complex, intense flavours of dark fruits, spices with earthy undertones.
‘Simon, I’m worried.’
‘Of course, you are. This is…abnormal.’
‘But what if we can’t get food. Or water. Or worse?’

‘Amy, they won’t let us starve. Hungry people riot. Scared people want certainty. Comfortable people comply. The solution will arrive fast because it has to. They’ll move quickly. Not out of compassion. Out of control. Comfort is the mechanism. Comfort needs infrastructure. And guess what? The infrastructure is already installed.’
I place my thumb on my phone.
‘Beep. Payment accepted.’
I wait for a reply that doesn’t come, The Chemical Brothers racing around my brain.
Sometimes I feel that I’m misunderstood
The phone buzzes at a quarter to nine. ARC, the teal ding, not the klaxon. The PM will address the nation at nine.
Amy takes a sip of wine. Puts her glass on the side table. Sits cross-legged and turns to face me.
‘What do you think he’ll say?’
I put another log on the fire.
‘I think he’ll say Be well.’

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — PM ADDRESS — 21:00 GMT — 19 FEBRUARY 2027

paras.t: Good evening.

I was due to address you at six o’clock this evening. Shortly before that broadcast, at approximately half past five, financial systems across twenty-three nations experienced a further phase of disruption. The United Kingdom is one of those nations. I took the decision to delay this address so that I could instead chair an emergency COBRA session and speak to my counterparts in the affected nations. I wanted to come to you with information, not speculation.
Here is what we know.

The restoration of payment and banking services that had been progressing well over the past forty-eight hours has suffered a significant and unexpected setback. Our current assessment is that a second phase of the original attack was embedded within the systems themselves, and was triggered by the process of reconnection. The National Cyber Security Centre is working through the night to establish the full technical picture.

As a precaution, cloud services that were in the process of being restored have been taken back offline. This includes platforms and services that were cleared and returned to operation earlier today. I understand the frustration of that. But until we understand the nature of what we are dealing with, we cannot leave those systems running. The NCSC has made this recommendation and I have accepted it.

I know many of you experienced this directly this evening. In shops. At terminals. On your phones. I know many of you have seen messages on your banking applications using the word “permanently.” I want to address that. Those messages were generated automatically by systems detecting that their connection to verified records has been interrupted. They describe a technical condition at this moment in time. They are not a statement of fact about your money and they are not a prediction.
I must be straightforward with you.
I told you on Monday that we were looking at days, not weeks. Last night I told you we were on track. That schools would reopen on Monday. That businesses would follow.

I cannot confirm that timetable tonight. We are, in many respects, back to where we were at the start of this week. The progress we made was real. The systems that were restored were functioning. What happened this evening does not undo the work that was done — but it does change the picture, and I need my security and technical advisers to complete their assessment before I can set out a new timetable. I will not give you a timeline I cannot stand behind.
Here is what has not changed.
Our essential services are unaffected. Hospitals are open. Emergency services are responding. Power, water and gas supplies are secure. The emergency measures already in place remain in place.
Schools will not reopen on Monday as planned. ARC Education will continue and we will update parents as the position becomes clearer.

For the time being, all non-essential travel should stop. Stay local. Stay close to your families. Check on your neighbours, particularly those living alone. If you need help, your local Community Recovery Hub remains open.

ARC Emergency and ARC Local will continue to provide live updates through the night and into tomorrow. My colleagues and I will address you again at nine o’clock tomorrow morning with a full assessment of where we stand.
This is a setback. It is a serious one. But we have the infrastructure, the people and the resolve to deal with it. We dealt with the first shock. We will deal with this one.
Stay safe. Stay local.

turns.title: PM Address · Day 5 Evening

paras.t: He didn’t say it.

Stay safe. Stay local. That’s how the PM ended. Not Be Well. I’d sat through all sixteen minutes waiting for those two words and they never came. Stay safe. Stay local. The same words from his first address, but inverted. Four days ago it was stay local, stay safe. Tonight he put safety first. Is safety no longer a given? The instruction has become a wish. I don’t want to think about what this might mean. I pray Dev has called it right that comfortable people comply. They’ll ensure discomfort is minimised. The dropping of Be Well is telling. Intentional. The man who’s held a nation together simply doesn’t forget his tidy little sign-off? What it means, I’m not quite sure. But underneath the composure, the COBRA-briefed steadiness, he was rattled. I could hear it. Amy could feel it. Be Well is what a system says. Tonight the system chose not to speak.
Amy turns the television off. The screen goes dark and the room is suddenly very quiet.
‘Bollocks. The market’s off, then,’ I say.
‘Yeah.’

I pick up my phone and start firing off texts. I’d already had thirty-odd traders calling, texting, demanding to know if the market was cancelled. Up to this point I’d assumed we’d have to, but hadn’t committed either way. The PM address confirmed it. Shops and supermarkets will not open tomorrow. All other businesses, hospitality and leisure venues remain closed until further notice. If it were my decision alone, I’d have opened regardless. But the council would take a dim view of such bravado.
Most traders understood it was out of my control and replied with ‘thought as much’ or a thumbs up emoji. Cheryl replied asking who would refund her for all the cakes she’s baked and couldn’t sell.

The dogs have settled. Olive’s on her bed, Wilf’s pressed against Amy’s legs. The fire’s dying. We haven’t put another log on since the speech finished. The Pommard is finished. I don’t open another bottle. There’s nothing celebratory about this evening and there’s nothing to anaesthetise either. We passed through anaesthesia somewhere around half past five and came out the other side into something flatter, colder, numb. There’s no more Pommard either — nothing else would hit the spot after that.
A knock on the door. Wilf and Olive lift their heads but don’t bark. They know the knock. Only Kate could make a knock sound so cheery.

She’s standing on the doorstep in her parka, hood still up, face lit from below by her phone’s torchlight. ‘I saw your light on. I’m just back from the hub.’ She says it quickly, like someone who needs to be inside a house that isn’t hers.

Amy pulls out a chair at the kitchen table. She opens a bottle of red and pours a glass for Kate. She wraps both hands around it but doesn’t take a sip. Amy tops our glasses up too. There’s a reason now. An excuse. I have a swig. German Pinot Noir. a glugger. It’s fine.

Kate starts talking. Incessantly. A barrage. A very well-meaning and very polite barrage. She needs to let off steam. Amy and I clock this and simply listen. And sip. She’s not ranting about the architecture, the implications, about what any of this means or who the perpetrators might be. She’s recounting tales of Margaret. About the old chap who doesn’t understand why his iPad won’t work. About the woman with the walking stick who’d been telling another volunteer that her husband’s card had worked at Sainsbury’s that morning. Repeatedly. The same story again and again, but told with such joy.
‘They were happy,’ she says. ‘A sense of camaraderie.’
She takes her first sip of wine. A small one.
‘When I got there at three, they were actually happy. Comparing notes. Which cards worked. Which shops were open. Like sharing war stories. The cheerful, we’re-in-this-together ones.’
Her second sip, bigger this time. She cradles the glass.

‘Then the klaxon. We were in the hub kitchen. Two dozen of us around a table. Those with phones looked at them at the same time. The exact same movement. Those without phones looked mystified.’ Another sip. ‘Nobody said anything. For about a minute nobody said anything at all.’

Kate had stayed to comfort, to explain, to listen. She’d stayed to watch the PM’s speech with them. All of them, gathered around the telly in the community centre, listening to a man tell them that the progress was real but the picture has changed. Kate’s voice switched to a steadier pace and tone when recounting this part. Professional. Measured. She’s told this kind of story before. She deals in crisis narratives.

Then she says, a hint of melancholy in her tone — ‘Margaret. She’s there every day. She’s eighty-something. She brings biscuits. Margaret watched the whole thing and when it finished she patted the hand of the woman next to her.’
Well. It’s for the best, isn’t it. If they’re doing it properly this time, it’s for the best.

Kate puts her glass down. And that’s when she breaks. Not dramatically. No sound at first. Her face just…changes. Compresses. The professionalism drains out of it and what’s left is a woman at a kitchen table who’s emotionally spent from watching old people, kind people, be simultaneously frightened and grateful and accepting. Amy’s arm goes around her. I put my hand on her wrist. We don’t mention false flags or firmware or latent biometric systems or technocracy. We simply comfort our friend.

Kate finishes her wine. Wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand. ‘Sorry. Shit. Sorry. I’ve got a client at eight in the morning. Long-term. She’s..’ A pause. ‘This is not a good week for any of my patients.’
She gets up. A big group hug. She leaves. I lock the door behind her. The house settles. I text Mum, Sam, Emilia. And then bed.

Bed. There is nothing else. The bedroom is still warm despite the heating being off for nearly an hour. We get in. The sheets are cold. Refreshingly cold and crisp. Amy curls into me and I put my arm around her and we lie there in silence, listening to the house. A car passes — someone staying local.

I was right. I am right. Dev was right as were many more of our persuasion. Confirmed by the PM. Chapter Two as Rupert puts it. Financial records gone. Being right feels…wrong. A dark, specific, private, unnamable feeling. Inside. In my chest. In my fingertips. Not satisfaction. Not vindication. Something worse. A kind of relief. Because if nothing I do changes anything, then nothing I failed to do is my fault. I knew and I did nothing and the outcome is identical. The helplessness is perversely comfortable. It fits.
Amy rolls onto her side. Pulls the duvet up. Sighs.
‘We’ve been here before,’ she says. Quiet. Not a question. Not philosophical. Just tired.

I hear the faint hum of the extractor fan in the bathroom. I’ve become more aware of the nighttime sounds of the house in the past few days. The radiator clicking. Cooling metal contracting. A slow, rhythmic click. I focus on it. I don’t mean to focus on it. The click becomes a tick. Hypnotic. The gap between the ticks getting longer as the metal cools. Or shorter. I can’t tell any more whether I’m counting or being counted.
It’s for the best…

Six-thirty-three. The heating hasn't come on yet. The bedroom is cold. The timer is set for seven - yet to click into action. Instinctively, I pick up my phone to open the Hive app so I can give the heating a manual boost - and soon realise, like all apps it’s un-openable, functionally useless. Dead.
Amy’s side of the bed is empty. Empty and cold. Her pillow is cold too. Not recently-left to go for a wee cold, but properly cold. She's been gone a while.

I lie still for a moment. A dream lingering, not in my thoughts, not as an image but as a feeling - an intangible low hum. It fades as the room comes into focus. The picture of the wall by my side of the bed - a wedding collage that’s just the right side of cheesy - I think. A stack of cream velvet cushions on the floor - daytime aesthetics that become nighttime inconvenience. The curtains - a small chink of something that isn’t total gloom appearing through a chink in them. The shape of an ordinary Saturday morning.
The hallway is dark but there's light coming from the kitchen. I follow it.

Amy is sitting at the table in her dressing gown, both hands around her favourite mug - a Kinta stoneware mug handmade in Vietnam - I think the official description of the colour is ivory and mustard. It’ll be full of Earl Grey. Her third cup of the morning based on the used teabags sitting on a side-plate by the kettle. The dogs are at her feet. The kitchen has that particular warmth of a room where the kettle has been boiled more than once. She looks up.
'You were making noises.'
I fill the kettle. 'What kind of noises?'

'Talking. Sort of. Like you were having a conversation with someone. And then - this sounds mad - booing. Jeering. Like you were at a pantomime or something.' She pauses. 'And then nothing. Completely still. For ages. I nearly woke you.'
'How long have you been up?'
'Half five. Couldn't sleep.'

I drop a teabag into a mug. I have a matching Kinta mug. Perhaps not matching. A companion piece. It’s black. Matt black with glossy band is the official description. The kettle boils. The click of the kettle switch is the loudest thing in the house.

'Weird dream,' I say, stating the obvious. I leave it at that, because whatever it was - and it was definitely something - something I can’t quite get the shape of yet. And even if I could, I wouldn’t be able to put it into words at half six in the morning. Not yet. Not before a cup of tea.

My blood glucose level is good. Flat arrow overnight. I take 4 units of insulin. The tea and the dawn phenomenon will send it spiking without some injected Fiasp. The small rituals of a body that has been monitored by a sensor for years now. I have no idea how I coped for decades without continuous monitoring and never-ending finger pricks.

The heating fires at seven. Amy has been sitting in the cold. I don’t tell her she could have turned it on from the thermostat on the wall. The boiler clicks on and the house is filled with the sound of radiator ticks. The same ticking from last night. The hum again. Just for a second.
The house warms around us.

Amy puts her mug down. 'You know what's weird? We've got no idea what's happening out there. Not really. It's just us, this house, the neighbours, a few texts, family and close friends, Waitrose, a few shops and pubs. The Prime Minister and an app giving us the single source of truth.’
I cringe at the memory of Covid-era Jacinda Ardern. Unless you hear it from us, it is not the truth.
‘Unthinking respect for authority is the greatest enemy of truth.’ I pluck an Einstein quote from somewhere before my first sip of tea.
‘Sounds like something Dev would say,’ Amy replies - half-statement, half-question.
‘Einstein’ I reply.
We giggle.

'Do we ever know what’s going on out there? Really? We’re drip-fed whatever the algorithm decides to shove under our noses. How much of what we thought we knew was actually…’ I wave my hands theatrically whilst thinking for the right way to put it… 'Curated. Selected. Engagement-optimised bullshit. One big psyop?’
'That's different though. At least there was more than one source of bullshit.'
We simultaneously make the same sound, somewhere between a scoff and a laugh.

'Maybe this is how it's supposed to be,' I continue. 'Small communities. Local. Your actual neighbours, not social media bollocks with a bot or people you've never met. There's a number, it’s called…what is it?’
I’m racking my brains. ‘Hold on, it’ll come to me.’
‘It doesn’t matter what it’s called, just tell me what it is,’ Amy is getting impatient.
‘No, I want to remember it, hold on…’
I tap my index finger on the table rhythmically in an attempt to speed up the thought process.
‘Got it. Dunbar’s number’ I say triumphantly.
Amy looks at me, none the wiser.

‘Dunbar’s number. A hundred and fifty. That's the number of people you can actually hold a meaningful relationship with. After that, everyone's just a name. We've probably got about a hundred and fifty. Family, friends, people from the market, work, neighbours. That’s a community. A real one.'
'A hundred and fifty,' Amy says, her eyes glazed over as if she’s totting them up.

'Give or take. The point is - maybe we're not supposed to know what's happening in Manchester and Chicago and wherever else. Not from an anthropological perspective. Our brains aren’t wired for it. Maybe the everything-connected, always-online world is an aberration, and this - I gesture at the kitchen, the dogs, the Kinta mugs, the quiet - 'is actually closer to how we are supposed to live.'

The dogs shift position at Amy's feet with a synchronised huff. Outside, the sky is slowly becoming a brighter shade of grey. A blackbird starts singing. Amy’s favourite bird. We had one that nested in the garage at our old house. We had to leave the door open permanently for her. She was so tame, so beautiful. She became a family member, a friend. Part of our Dunbar number for sure.

'But that's the thing,' Amy says. She puts her mug down. 'We're happy. I mean, all things considered, sitting here, right now, I'm alright. You're alright. The kids are fine. Mum's fine. Jamie and Rupert are OK. And it's nice. The quiet. No pings, no scrolling, no constant barrage. It's actually been lovely.' She pauses. 'But what about everyone else? Are people in Birmingham sitting in their kitchens feeling like this? Or is there chaos. Panic. Actual panic. Rioting. Things we just haven't heard about because we can't hear about them.'
I pause to consider. The blackbird has encountered something that is causing her excitement. A worm?

‘That’s the flip side isn’t it? The yin to the yang of peace, the community and the isolation that feels wholesome. We’re so conditioned to needing to know, to having our finger on the pulse, that we feel lost without it. Bereft. Incomplete. Part of me really wanted to get back online. The knowledge vacuum has been freaking me out. No X to scroll through. Warts and all. I was genuinely excited to see what the Substacks were saying. See if anyone had actually worked out what happened. And then…’ I click my fingers.
'And then…I don't know if I'm disappointed or relieved.'
Amy looks at me, the that was a bit of a diatribe look. 'Both.'
'Both. Yeah.'
She picks up her mug again. ‘You’d soon get used to the rhythm of ‘living local’ I reckon’- Exaggerated air quotes - an annoying habit she’s picked up from me. ‘Less connected but more connected.’
I know exactly what she means.

She continues - ’If you broke the world down into little pockets - small communities, growing food, everyone looking after each other and their own patch - I think we’d be happier. I know it sounds a bit Good Life.’
‘It sounds like the Dunbar number made manifest.’ I cringe at my slightly wanky language.
‘Surely this is the way God made us?’ She visibly stops herself air-quoting God. ‘Humanity’s default. Everything you need within touching distance. People would be happier, I’m sure?’
‘Sounds like a 15 minute city,’ I say with a wry smile.
Amy looks at her phone. ’Just over an hour until the PM gives us the single source of truth.’
I take a sip of tea.
Nothing further to add, M’lud.
The blackbird makes a very high-pitched whistle. Amy recognises it straight away as the response to predators.
She jumps up to go into the garden to investigate.
‘Could be a magpie,’ she says. ‘Bloody bastards.’

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — JOINT ADDRESS — 09:00 GMT — 20 FEBRUARY 2027
turns.title: Joint Address · Day 6 Morning

paras.t: [STUB — Day 6. Hampers beginning. Fuel rationed. New routine: queue, walk dogs, try to keep sane. Kate volunteers at hub clinic. Amy's parents 45 mins away, Amy worrying. Amy's brothers off-grid. Dev: 'Not restoration. Replacement.']

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — PM ADDRESS — 18:00 GMT — 20 FEBRUARY 2027
turns.title: PM Address · Day 6 Evening

paras.t: The screen holds for a moment after he finishes. The seal. The flag. Then black.
Amy doesn't say anything. She picks up her tea. It'll be cold by now. She drinks it anyway.

I don't know what I expected. Something. An admission, maybe. A flicker of honesty behind the rehearsed concern and the carefully modulated pauses. What we got was a man in a good suit reading someone else's words in front of someone else's flag, telling us that everything was under control in a way that made it abundantly clear that nothing was under control.
And that this was, in fact, the point.

The map was a nice touch. The national recovery hub map. Clean. Colour-coded. Teal dots for open hubs, gold for opening soon. It looked like a weather forecast. Friendly and reassuring and designed to make you feel that someone, somewhere, was across it. Three thousand and something. More by morning. The Prime Minister had gestured at it with the practised ease of a man who had never set foot in a community centre in his life.
I pick up my phone.
ARC Local. The app that didn't exist eight days ago and now runs half the country. Auto-detected location. It knows where I am. Of course it does.
The national map was abstract. A screensaver for the anxious. This is not abstract.
Mid & East Sussex Recovery Hubs.

There they are. My towns. Lewes. Uckfield. Crowborough. Haywards Heath. The dots scattered across the Weald like a rash. I zoom in. Burgess Hill. Heathfield. Battle. The familiar geography rendered in satellite green and ARC teal.

One hundred and one hubs open. One hundred and one church halls, leisure centres, school gyms and community rooms pressed into service as distribution points for a system that materialised fully formed, as if from nowhere, in less than a week. Target by 0800 tomorrow: one hundred and forty-three.
Brighton and Hove has twenty-two. Wealden has nineteen. Hastings sixteen. Even Rother, which struggles to keep a post office open, has eight.
I scroll east. Bexhill. Eastbourne. The coast peppered with dots. Each one a place I've driven past or walked through or cursed at for its one-way system. Each one now a node in something. A network.

Sixty more gold dots. Opening within 24 hours. Not being built. Being opened. Because they were already built. Or at least the infrastructure was. The registration points. The distribution routes. The capacity allocations. Kate said the hub she's been volunteering at took delivery of forty brand-new iPads yesterday. Military drop-off. Still in cellophane. Each box coded with a hub reference number she didn't recognise. Nobody told her what they were for. The number matched the capacity of the building exactly.
Amy leans over. She looks at the screen. She doesn't say anything for a while.
'That's a lot of dots.'
'One hundred and sixty-one by tomorrow morning. Just for our bit of Sussex.'
She processes this. Amy processes things differently to me. I catastrophise and connect. She absorbs and waits. When she's ready, she speaks. And when she speaks, she's usually right.
'How do they know where to put them?'
'The PM said local authorities and emergency—'

'No. How do they know. How do they know that Heathfield needs a hub and where to put it. How do they know the capacity for Wealden versus Rother. This isn't improvised, Simon. You don't allocate capacity by district in six days. You do it in six days if you already had the plan.'
I look at her.
She looks at the screen.
The dogs stir. Wilf does that thing where he repositions his entire body by moving one leg. Olive doesn't move at all but somehow ends up closer to the radiator.
'Dev would love this,' I say.
'Dev would already have it archived and annotated.'
She's not wrong.

I take a screenshot of the map to send to Dev. Lewes to Rye. One hundred and one dots of teal. Sixty dots of gold. A network that appeared like infrastructure always appears when it's been planned for years — suddenly, and all at once, and with a colour scheme.
I prepare to send it to Dev. I remember I can only send words, no photos.
I write a text instead. Quite cryptic.
He'll get it.
Simon reveals he’s been writing. A short story. Using AI. ‘It just seemed to flow.’ The knowing-doing gap performed: he’s handed his threat model to the machine and he’s showing you the output.

The night before money arrives. Tinned tomato soup, toast from frozen bread, tea. The fridge has insulin, butter, and half a lemon. Amy’s been at the hub all day. Simon watches BBC — the same three experts saying ‘unprecedented’ in slightly different configurations. He turns it off. Checks ARC Emergency instead. Reads the same information in a third of the time. Doesn’t notice the preference forming.

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — JOINT ADDRESS — 12:00 GMT — 21 FEBRUARY 2027
turns.title: PM & Chancellor · Day 7 Noon

paras.t: Two o’clock. Simon goes to Tesco. The queue starts in the car park. Not panicked — orderly, British, resigned. Soldiers in the car park directing traffic, high-vis over camo. Inside: shelves patchy but bread and milk and tins in decent supply. The beep. Simon holds his phone to the terminal. ARC EMERGENCY — PAYMENT CONFIRMED — BALANCE: £131.40. He’s bought bread, milk, eggs, pasta, tinned tomatoes, teabags, dog food, paracetamol, and a bottle of wine.
The steady-state address. Restoration proceeding. Hubs operational. The last broadcast Simon watches before going deeper.

The deeper disconnection. No internet, no feed, no algorithm. Dogs get longer walks. Meals take longer. Simon writes E2 on local AI. The sky is noticed. Something beautiful is happening inside the crisis.

Amy leaves at 7am for the hub. Hamper distribution starts at 8. George is on Instagram — it came back yesterday afternoon. The crisis is the content. Everyone posting their Dark Month experience. Empty shelf photos. Hamper queue selfies. The algorithm doing what it always does. WhatsApp is alive. A text from Simon’s mum sent at 11pm on Valentine’s Day: ‘Hope you had a lovely evening darling xxx.’ Sent before the Event. Arriving now.

The first chapter that compresses time. EPM Week 2 refresh: another £200 drops into the phone. A push notification. Simon sees it, swipes it away, tells Amy over dinner. Already normalised. Six days from ‘the Chancellor has put money in your hands’ to swiping away the notification like a Deliveroo promo. The PM does a midweek address. Simon doesn’t watch it. He sees the ARC push summary while making coffee. Doesn’t turn the telly on.
Time marked on paper. The calendar on the fridge becomes the central document. Amy’s handwriting. Simon’s additions in pencil.

Dev’s forensic dump arrives at 2am. The Signal channel goes from short probes to a wall of text. ARC timeline analysis. AIDA architecture matching a DARPA proposal from 2019. The FCA interoperability mandate. The procurement contracts. Amy comes downstairs. Reads it over Simon’s shoulder. Neither of them speaks for a while. Then Amy says something practical — ‘What are we supposed to do with this?’ Simon doesn’t have an answer.

The dead zone. Dev’s forensic dump is a week old. Simon has read it three times. He can’t verify it, can’t dismiss it, can’t act on it. Social media is fully operational. The conversation has moved from ‘what happened’ to ‘what’s next.’ Half of it matches what Dev sent him. The other half is conspiracy noise he can’t distinguish from the signal. Amy comes home from the hub: ‘You’re doing the thing again.’ ‘What thing?’

[STUB — Day 26–30. The language shifts. PM Week 3: 'The old system failed us.' Nobody says 'back to normal' anymore. Kate notices registration equipment at community centres. Cash nearly exhausted. BBC running 'what might the new system look like' segments. The country stops waiting to go back and starts waiting to go forward.]

[STUB — Day 31–35. The anticipation week. BBC speculation on new system. Hubs being fitted with registration equipment — Kate notices. Cash virtually gone. PM expected to address nation ‘within days.’ 23 nations confirm coordinated announcement. Schools ready to reopen within 48 hours. The build-up.]
The protests. Multiple factions, contradictory agendas. The whole family goes.

[STUB — Day 35. HEAVY — centrepiece turn. PM prime time. International simulcast. Seven beats: old system broken → ARC survived → AIDA → THE DEBT JUBILEE → registration open → not temporary → 23 nations. Amy's eyes when the mortgage disappears. Street parties. Neighbours hugging. The gratitude is seismic, genuine, earned. Dev mesh: 'speech metadata. created 9 feb. six days before the attack.' Amy's inner voice: 'God help me, yes.']
Registration. Jubilee. Debt cancelled. UBI. The PM stands up for the first time in a month.

[STUB — Day 36–37. Registered vs unregistered contrast. Amy's mum sends hamper photos. George: 'Mum, can I just register? I'm 19.' He does. 'Dad, it's just an app.' Simon finds out via AIDA notification. BritCoin first allocation: 10,000 BC/adult.]

[STUB — Day 38–42. Sam and Emilia registered by their mum. 'Your ex texted.' The knife that isn't AIDA — it's his ex-wife doing the right thing. Simon's rage/relief/grief. Mortgage showing £0.00. The horror of ease.]

[STUB — Day 49. Chloe in the kitchen doorway. 17. 'I'm literally the only person in my year who isn't registered.' She needs Simon's signature — under 18. The A-levels she's missing. Amy won't sign without Simon. AIDA learning platform genuinely excellent. Hub learning: worksheets.]

[STUB — Day 56. HEAVY. Kate from next door. Psychologist. Registered yesterday. Wine in the garden. 'I know what they're doing, Simon. The NLP in the speeches. The fear-reassurance cycle. I can see every stitch in the puppet strings.' She drinks. 'I registered anyway. Because seeing the strings doesn't make you less of a puppet. It just makes you a sad one.' Simon's mirror.]

[STUB — Day 63. Amy's brothers are holdouts. Rupert can't get his prescription. Jamie can't buy fuel. Amy's mum crying on the phone. Simon visits dad in care home — dad registered by institution, no consent. AIDA knows Simon through everyone else's data. Protest that evening: hundreds in a nation of 67 million. Police almost bored. 'Resistance is a luxury good.']

[STUB — Day 70. HEAVY — heart of the game. After the teenagers have gone upstairs. Dogs on the kitchen floor. Kettle boiling. Amy: 'Where's the mass, Simon?' The conversation. Not screaming — quiet, tired, honest. Dev on mesh: 'Don't do it.' AIDA: 'We're here when you're ready, Simon.' It used his name. 'We'll go tomorrow. Together.']
She said nothing. She played Northern Sky by Nick Drake. We hugged. We cried. We left for the Community Recovery Hub.

I never felt magic crazy as this
I never saw moons, knew the meaning of the sea
I never held emotion in the palm of my hand
Or felt sweet breezes in the top of a tree
But now you're here
Brighten my northern sky
Mid Morning
It was the discussion on everyone's lips. But ask the majority if they were registering you'd get a bemused look. What do you mean if?

On the face of it who could argue? Debts erased, £1000 per month (well 1000 Brits, same same), food hampers. And hampers they were. A far cry from ration books and make-do-and-mend. Fresh, healthy, tailored to your dietary requirements, customisable, delivered to your door. And free. And for what, registering on a 'new App'.
They simply couldn't be made to see the downside. Or they refused to acknowledge it. As Cypher said, 'ignorance is bliss'.
Some could see it, of course. We'd been on the protests. I'd say there were more there than there were for the Lockdown marches.
Amy could see it. Of course she could. Or perhaps she felt it — that would be more accurate. Some things she simply understood.
Very female. Very Amy. Not knowledge. Intuition.
I'd put in the hard yards. Hour upon hour of research and 'deep dives'. Over a decade's worth. I had a file on them and they sure as hell had a file on me. They had a file on everyone.
Why are they doing this? She simply couldn't comprehend evil. But she knew there was a 'they'.

She'd be in floods of tears if she saw a dead deer on the road. It's not fair that this beautiful creature must die. I would be upset, but that was the way of the world. I didn't have her empathy. Not many did.
This however, this was beyond her comprehension. I responded with rage. She responded with sadness. Infinite sadness.
I didn't know what to say, what to do. I knew what was going on. Well I thought I did. I used to think I did. I was having my doubts. What if this is just progress, what if it's just better.
Karma police, arrest this man

I'd bombarded her, everyone and anyone who'd listen, with my 'research'. Sent links to essays by investigative journalists, punchy truth movement YouTube videos. Shown them scientific papers. I had a bulging digital file of them. I had half-read paperbacks exposing the whole nine yards. I'd talked about neo-feudalism, transhumanism, satanism, spiritual warfare, prophecy of the Third Temple, eschatology, eugenics. The list goes on. And on. I'd even jokingly prepared a conspiracy-nutter style presentation on a whiteboard, joining the dots with string. Some listened. Some shrugged. Some stared blankly. Some laughed. Many asked who are 'they'?

I'd tell all my friends, but they'd never believe me
They'd think that I'd finally lost it completely

Yet here I was. Already AIDA registered. Clean, easy, quick. 1000 Brits in my wallet. Soon to be several thousand more once we've presented our statements at the 'Community Recovery Hub'. You couldn't make this shit up. But someone did. They did. Oh, plus the house. In our name. No mortgage.
Soon they'll call our names and ask 'papers, please?'

What else can I be?
All apologies

cards.ttl:
Firmware pushes I can verify independently:

🇬🇧 UK — 18–19 Jan. Ingenico/Verifone. 2.1M terminals. Biometric template storage confirmed.
🇺🇸 USA — 19–20 Jan. Verifone/Square POS fleet. Scope unknown. NESARA noise burying real data.
🇯🇵 Japan — 22 Jan. JCB-affiliated NFC terminals. Biometric + vein-pattern storage.
🇧🇷 Brazil — 19 Jan. Cielo POS network. Simultaneous with UK push.
🇦🇺 Australia — 21 Jan. CBA merchant terminals. Limited deployment.

Same encrypted callback. Same dormant container. Same BIS routing. Same biometric template format across all five. I am not making a claim about what this means. I am telling you what is there.
cards.snip: Five countries. No Germany — even though he’d bet his house the German push was real too. The fake whistleblower killed that data point for good. And the US data is half-buried under Q mythology. Vedmore’s done the work. Four hundred likes. Gone by morning.
